9321: Protection against bewitchment with a cross of sand on the inside of the front and back doors. A case of a cloth in a bed tick in which feathers were stuck with the points upward, in the shape of a heart. The cloth was burnt to give the sorceress burns and rob her of her rest.
9517: A farmhand who can see into the future sees one night a dead person lying in the straw, covered with a shroud. Because it is too dark to see who it is, he cuts off a lock of hair at the right temple. The next day he sees that he himself is missing a lock of hair. He now knows that things will end badly for him. He goes to work at another farm. He forgets what he saw that night. Years later he meets his old master again. He is invited for a meal. During the meal he collapses. He is laid in the straw on the threshing floor and covered with a shroud.
9527: A hunter sees a hare cross the road every day. He never manages to hit the animal. A farmer advises him to put three grains of rye in with the shot. The next day he hits the hare. But the shot is not fatal and the animal escapes. Together with the farmer he follows the trail of blood. It leads to the house of the sick neighbour woman. The neighbour got better, and no one ever saw the hare again.
9538:
An old farmer on his way home is suddenly pushed off the road. He stands still in amazement. Then he sees a cart approaching drawn by two horses, a brown one and a black one. The driver and the people walking with the cart are dressed in black. They are going to the churchyard. The farmer wonders who is being buried with such a mismatched team of horses. When he gets home he tells his wife the story.
Not long afterwards an old man dies. At the funeral the wagon is drawn by a brown and a black horse. The peat bog is so marshy that the horses must wear wooden blocks on their hooves to keep from sinking in. The second black horse had resisted having the trippen (wooden hoof blocks) tied on. That is why it had to be replaced by a brown horse.
11563: The duivelssteen (devil's stone) is a stone that marked the boundary between the marken (common lands) of De Lutte and Zuid-Berghuizen. One evening a woman walked past the stone with her shopping, but did not cross herself as she passed, although this was the custom. Suddenly a man is walking beside her who behaves very politely and carries her shopping, for he says: "Madam, this burden is too heavy for you." When a little later they cross the post road, there is suddenly a bang and the man disappears in a cloud of sulphur fumes. It had been the devil.
13091: A headless calf haunts the area. It tinkles like glass and at a certain moment it collapses. Whoever looks at the calf loses his good health for ever.
13097: A father and son live in a hole under the ground. To rob and murder passers-by, they stretch a rope with a bell across the road so they can hear passers-by. One day a girl comes by. The son does not want to kill her because he wants her as his wife. For a year father and son never leave the girl alone, but after a year they have to go out together after all. The girl manages to escape. The son runs after her and throws an axe at her, but he misses. The girl tells the schout (sheriff) everything, and the two murderers are beheaded. At the spot where the two murdered so many people, the victims still haunt as witte wieven (white women).
13111: In Zwartsluis it is the custom at the launching of a ship that the schoolchildren may be on board. One time, however, the head of the shipyard finds this too time-consuming. But the ship will not leave the yard, whatever is tried. The strongest man in the area advises letting the children back on the ship first, and then the ship will go into the water by itself. And so it happens.
13113: A man has sold his soul to the devil. Unlike all the other poor farmers, he has plenty of money. Every night he fights with the devil. The last time the man wins and throws the devil to the other side.
13130: A father and son live in a hole under the ground. To rob and murder passers-by, they stretch a rope with a bell across the road so they can hear passers-by. One day the son takes a girl captive. She has to shave the father every day. Once, when the son is away, she cuts the father's throat and flees. The son pursues her, but she is safe inside a house. The axe mark in the threshold is still a reminder of this.
13162: An alderman is herding sheep when he sees a house on fire. He crosses a river by boat to reach the house, but when he stands in front of it, there is no fire to be seen. Later it turns out the man had a clairvoyant vision, for that house actually burned down a number of years later.
13163: Two labourers see a white ghostly apparition in human form. When they say good evening to it, the apparition suddenly vanishes.
13240: Werewolves can be killed or cured by shooting a silver dime at them with a gun, or by first cutting into the ground with a knife. The narrator's father once fought with a werewolf.
13241: A young man is a werewolf. His friends want to play a trick on him. At a birthday party they do not let him leave. Suddenly a wolfskin falls down the chimney into the fire. It burns and the young man is freed.
13278: A man who moved a boundary stone must wander about after his death. Only when he receives the answer "where you took it from" to his question "where shall I put the stone?" is he released.
13289: At a wedding one of the guests remarks that they forgot to invite the witte wieven (white women). When someone mockingly calls out to the witte wieven, an axe is thrown at his head. He just manages to flee inside in time. The door still shows the marks of the axe. The witte wief (white woman) calls out that she could have caught him if she had not lost her little shoe.
13391: A farmer sees a hare sitting on his land. He takes his gun to shoot the hare, but after every shot the hare runs on, laughing. The farmer spends the whole Sunday chasing the hare, but he cannot catch it. Because of this he misses all the Sunday masses. The hare must surely have been the devil, who wanted to keep the farmer away from church.
13394: On the way, a cat jumps onto a horse pulling a cart. The horse has to stop and can only go on once the cat has been knocked off. The next day an injured person reveals who the cat was.
13395: A woman can change into a cat and can also get in when the door is shut. Once the cat is struck by a man; the next day the woman walks about with a cloth around her head.
13396: A tree grower is suspected of being a sorcerer. For once he gives apples to a family, and they come alive once they are in the family members' stomachs. After the family members have drunk a few good gulps of horse urine, the apples are "dead".
13398: When a man is on his way to his girlfriend one evening, a foal comes walking beside him. When the man raises his stick, the foal disappears, but each time he lowers his stick again, the foal is back.
13409: Two men walk to the village early in the morning to go threshing. Two creatures with big eyes walk along with them. The men try to chase them away, but the creatures keep walking with them.
13538: A farmhand who turns into a wolf at night disappears when the farmer finds a wolfskin under his bed and burns it.
13619: Someone sees and hears trains and ships passing over the land. Later a railway line and a canal are built there.
13620: The stiepelteken (mark in the doorpost) came about when a wit wief (white woman) threw the axe with which she was chasing a farmhand, and it landed in the doorpost of the barn door. The farmhand had challenged the witte wieven (white women) by bringing a spit to a spinning gathering and immediately running off again.
13621: A farmhand passes the Witte Wieven (white women) and challenges them. One of them chases him all the way home. He just manages to flee inside. But she throws a club at the door, breaking off a piece of the stiepel (doorpost).
13622: A farmhand makes a bet that he will bring the spit to the Witte Wieven (white women). One of them chases him. The farmhand just manages to flee into a house. The axe the Witte Wief (white woman) threw lands in the stiepel (doorpost). The Witte Wief could not run faster because she had trouble with one of her shoes.
13623: A farmhand brings the spit to the Witte Wieven (white women). One of them chases him. The farmhand just manages to flee into a house. The axe the Witte Wief (white woman) threw lands in the stiepel (doorpost). The Witte Wief could not run faster because she had trouble with one of her shoes.
13624: A farmhand walks past the Witte Wieven (white women) at night. Because he insults them, one of them chases him. The farmhand just manages to flee into a house. The axe the Witte Wief (white woman) threw lands in the stiepel (doorpost).
13629: A farmer is making hay with his sons. Because a thunderstorm seems to be coming, they pack up early and go home. However, they leave their bacon pancakes, brought in a red handkerchief, behind for the witte wieven (white women). When they come to the field the next day, the pancakes are gone and all the hay has been put into stacks.
13632: The mare can attack horses and people at night. With horses, the mare makes their manes tangled together. With people, the mare crawls onto their chest, so that the sleeper feels very oppressed, has horrible dreams and breaks out in a sweat. To ward off the mare from horses, the manes must be cut off with a bread knife. To ward it off from people, clogs or shoes must be placed in front of the bed with the opening facing the bed.
13635: A wit wief (white woman) is known for luring young farmers' sons to her dwelling. A poor farmer's son knows the rhyme that can break her power and goes to her. At the crucial moment, however, he has forgotten the rhyme. Still, he returns with a bag full of gold. He marries the daughter of a rich farmer. Because the farmer's son is still in the white woman's power, his wife thinks up a plan. She dresses as a boy and lets the white woman chase her. In this way the white woman crosses the border of her territory and falls into the hands of a man who manages to drown her.
13636: A drunken farmhand wants to tease the witte wieven (white women). Sitting on a horse, he throws a hair-pin among them. Immediately the women chase him with the flashing hair-pin. They throw the hair-pin at him, but he escapes because it gets stuck in the door.
13638: A road is known as a haunted road. In the evening and at night a white woman can be seen on it, with long, silky hair. Her dress is covered with feathers. Often in the morning some of these little feathers can be seen lying on the road. Her presence seems to have a fatal influence.
13761: The narrator has noticed little of witchcraft; has once seen a little light at the spot where a house was later built in which a night light burns.
13762: A person born with a caul has to get up at night; foresees a funeral procession; sees a train running before the railway is built.
13765: Where a fireball turns into a fire is an omen that a barn will be built on that spot. Later ball lightning causes a fire in the barn.
13770: The narrator's opinion on belief in ghosts and witches, and how that belief arises.
13771: Haunted house where doors open and close by themselves. The narrator believes other events in the haunted house have nothing to do with ghosts. Others believe it was never right there and that earlier strange phenomena were bad omens.
13772: Seeing a little light is a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a drowning, a murder, the building of houses.
13773: Women believe a sick cow is dying through bewitchment; they chase away the first person who comes the next day and make a new entrance to the hut, placing a scythe to keep the witch and the devil out.
14752: The devil follows a woman on her way home in the evening.
14792: In the evening a big dog, which a man believes is the devil, will not let him take his bicycle.
14793: A hunter believes he has met the devil, because every time he tries to shoot a hare that runs in circles around him, the gun refuses to fire.
14796: After a man discovers that the man he is playing cards with has horse's hooves, he drops his card, as was always done when the devil was in the game, and leaves.
14799: At midnight a man sees no one who can ferry him across, and the boat is on the other side. As soon as he has asked the devil for help, the unmanned boat comes to him and takes him across.
14800: A man who keeps playing cards has had trouble with the devil all his life. One evening he is chased by the devil right into his house and fights with the devil.
14801: The farmhand of a skipper who swears a lot sees a black-haired devil appear on the ship and go into the forecastle. The farmhand hears screaming and finds the skipper completely blue.
14802: A man passes a farm at night where witte wieven (white women), witches and others, and even the devil, are feasting and drinking. When he calls out that he would like a drink too, the party stops at once, and the witte wieven and witches come at him and chase him. He escapes by jumping into a stream with his horse, for witte wieven cannot stand water.
14803: A barrel with a bluish light irresistibly draws a fishing boat towards it, so that changing course is impossible. The devil, who turns out to be sitting on the barrel, floats to the boat and disappears when a fisherman calls on the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Afterwards a smell of sulphur hangs over the boat and the catch is spoiled.
14808: Some people can make the jack of clubs from the deck of cards fetch a bottle of jenever (Dutch gin). When there are three knocks they must open the door at once, otherwise they die on the spot.
14809: During a card game all the bottles and glasses start rattling and a black cat flies through them.
14812: A girl who dances all evening and night with a gentleman keeps asking the time, because she has to go to church the next day. It turns out she has danced with the devil for so long that she has missed the church service.
14814: The expression Van nie'j Argelo, meaning having to do something over again, is said to come from the devil's words asking to redo the fight after he had lost it to farmer Argelo.
14816: A bet that the jack of clubs, tied to an empty bottle, can bring a full bottle. Someone makes his face pale, reads from a book with a red cover and at a sign puts the bottle outside the door. After a few minutes there are three knocks; the person must open the door and take the filled bottle from an entirely black figure.
14830: The devil accepts the gamekeeper's invitation to take a puff of his pipe, the double-barrelled shotgun, and puts both barrels in his mouth. The gamekeeper pulls the trigger; the devil blows out great clouds of smoke, says it is strong tobacco and disappears.
14831: A group of drinkers also sets down a glass for the devil. As soon as someone says the devil had better come quickly, there is a lot of rattling and noise, without anything to be seen. The drinkers are so frightened that they do not dare go home, do not go to church on Sunday, and never mock the devil again.
17317: Fastening a loose button on a coat or sewing on a new one must be done with the coat off, otherwise something will happen on the way.
22373:
An altar boy hears that sorcerers cannot leave the church if a dime that has first lain under a missal is placed under the threshold. When he tries it, the story turns out to be true. After mass some people stay in the church, and remain there until the dime is removed.
The priest advises the altar boy always to carry the dime with him, as protection against the sorcerers' revenge. But when the altar boy gets married, he forgets to put the dime in his wedding suit. He is attacked and killed by witches.
22377:
A farmhand has to mow grass for his master together with a day labourer. Because he eats so much, the maid brings him a bucket of soup and a bucket of green beans at midday. After the meal the farmhand suggests to the day labourer that they take a nap. The day labourer agrees, but he does not quite trust the farmhand and secretly stays awake.
The farmhand lies on his back with his mouth open, and at a certain moment a mole crawls out of it. The mole goes after the cows in the meadow and then crawls back. The farmhand stretches and gets up. But then he has to vomit. The day labourer sees him throwing up blood. The farmhand goes home and the day labourer goes to sow the grass. Later the farmer says that a calf has gone missing.
When the farmhand has died, the coffin is so heavy that nobody can lift it. The minister cannot do anything about it either. They fetch the priest. He has a rope and a book with him and walks around the coffin reading. People suspect he does this to drive away the evil spirits. Now the coffin can be lifted and taken to the churchyard.
22378:
A farmhand has to mow grass for his master together with a day labourer. Because he eats so much, the maid brings him a bucket of soup and a bucket of green beans at midday. After the meal the farmhand suggests to the day labourer that they take a nap. The day labourer agrees, but he does not quite trust the farmhand and secretly stays awake.
The farmhand lies on his back with his mouth open, and at a certain moment a mole crawls out of it. The mole goes after the cows in the meadow and then crawls back. The farmhand stretches and gets up. But then he has to vomit. The day labourer sees him throwing up blood. The farmhand goes home and the day labourer goes to sow the grass. Later the farmer says that a calf has gone missing.
When the farmhand has died, the coffin is so heavy that nobody can lift it. The minister cannot do anything about it either. They fetch the priest. He ties a rope to the coffin and pulls it from its place. Now the coffin can be lifted and taken to the churchyard.
22379:
A mother has a sick little daughter who will not get better. She fears the worst and checks the pillow. The feathers are stuck together in the shape of a wreath, so the child is bewitched. The mother fetches a priest.
The priest sits praying by the child until a witch comes by. He tells the witch to sit by the hearth. Once she sits there, she cannot leave. The priest threatens to have her burned if she does not cure the child. It turns out the witch has dolls with pins in them. When all the pins have been removed from the doll, the girl is well again.
22384: A man makes a bet that he dares to ask the wit wief (white woman) from the woods to dance. They dance until the man can go on no longer and drops dead.
22388: Two men are looking for grass stalks to cut. When they find none, they go home. After they have parted, one of the men suddenly sees a large wolf on his path. The next morning the other man asks him whether he saw the wolf.
22389: Two men are cutting grass stalks when one asks the other whether he would like to see him for once. Immediately a wolf is lying in the grass. The man never wants to work with the other again.
22395: When the farmers in Didam are churning, they do not like a witch to walk past, because then the milk will not turn to butter.
22397: On the Diemse heath lives a witch who can string pebbles on a thread.
22398: Someone wants to shoot a hare sitting in front of his house. But the bullet glances off every time. Then he shoots with a blessed bullet and hits the hare. It changes into an old woman, who is found bleeding in bed the next day.
22400: A beggar woman asks farmers for some flour. She almost always gets it. But nobody lets her near their small children, because she bewitches them.
22401: A woman has seven children, who all die right after birth. It is as if frogs shoot into their throats. This is because she has been bewitched. She moves to another village, where her eighth child does survive.
22404: Long ago a knight drowned in a canal in Den Haag. At night you can still see a little light burning above the lye water.
22407: A white sheep haunts the Pakop.
22411: A man goes to cut grass stalks with six others when the first man suddenly starts screaming. The group starts running. When they have stopped running, the first man tells them he saw a grijze juffer (grey lady).
22419:
You must never walk in the footsteps of someone who is no good.
A man is delivering meat when he is seized and thrown into the water. He will never know who did it.
22420:
A family has wood lying in the attic for lighting the school stove. At night a few men walk around. The wood is moved, but the men still manage to find it.
The family tells the municipality, which comes to clear away the wood. Then the haunting stops.
22427:
A cat keeps sitting at a man's window looking in. When he has had enough of it, he takes his gun and fires a shot, aiming at the cat. He hits the animal in the paw.
Over the following days the man notices that he no longer sees his neighbour woman, and he goes to her to see how she is. She is lying in bed with shot in her leg.
22432:
A man works in a factory in a neighbouring village. As he cycles to work, at a certain point he cannot get any further, however hard he pedals. It is as if something is holding his bicycle from behind. When he takes a different road, he has no trouble at all.
It is known that on the road he first took, a man who was once the ruler of the region lies buried together with his dog and a gun. The man thinks his experience has to do with the evil spirit of this man.
22434: A woman known as a witch invites her neighbours to a party. The neighbours think she can do magic. But since they will all be together, they are not afraid and go. After coffee and a drink, the neighbour tells her guests she will show them something. A spider comes down from the ceiling. The guests are frightened and want to run off. But the neighbour says everyone must stay seated; whoever leaves will die that very night.
22447: People are picked up by an invisible force and lifted over a house.
22449: Three white women always stand along a road. When a wagon drives along the road and the women take seven steps backward, the wagon cannot go on.
22453: A man defeats witchcraft: a foal that lets no one past on a footbridge, and a pack of cats (witches).
22454:
Several of a farmer's animals are found dead one morning. The farmer calls in the help of priests. They determine that the witchcraft comes from a certain house. They will return after fourteen days to help the farmer.
After the priests have helped the farmer, a woman will come to his door and offer him a flower. If he does not take the flower, the woman is set free and the farmer will no longer be troubled by anything.
22460: Dorus knew everything in advance. He would see a light and then he knew there would be a house there. He was also able to predict the houses on the heath that way, as well as the school.
22465: A woman sees a coffin; an omen of a death.
22466: A hare is shot at; the next day the neighbour woman turns out to be wounded - she is a witch.
22496: When the gun failed to fire at a hare or rabbit, people put a dubbeltje (ten-cent coin) on the gun. It bears the words: "God with us." Then the shot did go off and hit the hare. And the next day the woman who was said to practise witchcraft walked about with her arm in a sling.
22497: A horse stops in front of a house where there is witchcraft, and unloading the cart does not help. Then the farmer hacks a spoke out of the wheel, after which the horse is free. The next day they see that the woman (of the house), whom they accused of witchcraft, is walking lame.
22502: A farmer who worked with the devil was buried in the woods after his death in the shape of a devil, chained with a thick chain to an iron post.
22509: A woman who always goes to fetch paraffin late in the evening one time meets a ghost, a friar with a lamp in his hand, who follows her. The neighbour women advise her not to give him her hand, because then he will burn it off. The priest advised her to speak to him, which she did the next evening, whereupon the friar turns into a keeshond, which from then on regularly follows her.
22510: Two sisters' house is haunted and they send for a friar, who blesses the house and prays until he has mastered the devil. The devil turns into a billy goat, which the friar puts on a chain and leads through 's Herenberg. But nobody sees the goat; they only see the friar striking with a stick and sweating. He drags the goat across Stokkum to Van Drefeld's land in the woods and marks off a piece of ground for it, where the goat must stay. People are knocked off it by the goat. This happened to a shoemaker who one evening was delivering shoes to Stokkum, had had a drink and so ended up on the goat's ground. The goat butted him off the ground, and in his bewilderment the shoemaker went back to Wehl and has been afraid of the dark ever since.
22511: Grarus could not sleep and found a feather wreath in his pillow, which he believed was the work of a Jewish woman living in 's Herenberg who dealt in rags. He threw the wreath into boiling water and at that same moment sees the Jewish woman passing by. He wants to skewer her on his pitchfork, but is held back by his household. This Jewish woman is later said to have bewitched her husband; she visited him in prison, where he was held for smuggling, by crawling through the keyhole as a cat. After her death there was never any more witchcraft in 's Herenberg.
22513: A white lady haunts the area; she leaves alone people who do not provoke her and punishes those who mock her. Example of a carter who, invited to stay a while longer, mockingly replies that he still has to dance with the white lady that evening. On the way home the white lady comes towards him and he has to dance with her. Three days later he dies of exhaustion.
22514: A farmer who mocked the witte juffer (white lady) is punished. She turns his cart of heather upside down, but so gently that man and horse are unhurt.
22515: A white lady stamps her foot on the ground three times as a sign to the farmhand who is in her favour. He digs up an iron chest with great treasures. According to the narrator, the money went to the count.
22517: A man walking past the Kransjeswilg (an oak!) at night sees a white shape, hears the sound of teeth being ground and runs away fast.
22518: Dien goes from Didam with her sweetheart to the fair at Zeddam, and on the way through the woods the boy tells Dien to walk on slowly, because he has to go into the woods for a moment (to urinate). But instead of him a wolf comes out of the woods, bites her clothes and runs off again. Dien calls for help; a large piece has been torn out of her skirt. Then the boy arrives and Dien is glad to see him, but then she sees threads hanging from his mouth, threads from her skirt, and she realises he is a werewolf. She turns and runs back to Beek. She never sees the werewolf again.
22520: The Krenskeswilg, a pollarded oak near the Broekhuizen farm on the Hei in the Mark near Loerbeek, has a reputation for being haunted. The narrator was once at his girlfriend's in Loerbeek until late and went back to Beek around midnight; passing the Krenkeswilg he hears sighing and groaning and hurries on.
22521: The narrator was again visiting his girlfriend in Loerbeek and, under a full moon, passed the Broekhuizen farm by the Krenskeswilg, and sees a black man's head with two horns rise out of the (hollow) haunted tree up in front of the halo of the moon. He is so frightened that it shoots into his leg and he hurries off.
22522: The narrator often saw a light on the Hei at night that did not move like a vuurkerel (fiery man) and was stronger than a candle. So it must be a house that was yet to be built.
22524: Jan van Dees was coming back late from the mill over the Kerkdijk, and in the pitch dark his wheelbarrow slipped into a pit three times, and each time he lifted it a black cat got under his feet. He gives the beast an enormous kick, whereupon the witch says: "Do that again, Dees, and things won't go well for you," whereupon Jan quickly runs off as if the devil were after him.
22525: Bart, a boy from Beek, is going home from Zeddam late in the evening and his friends ask whether he is afraid of the boelekerel (bogeyman), but he says he is hurrying to see the Witte Juffer (White Lady) of the Berg, whom he wants to invite to dance with him at the Whitsun ale. When he reaches the Berg, he sees a white shade, the lady, who beckons him to stop. Then she comes to Bart, puts her arm around his waist and drags him into a round dance that draws all the strength out of him, and finally leaves him more dead than alive. His horse has walked home and the household come looking for him, find him at the foot of the Berg and bring him home, but after three days he dies.
22526: A poor man taking part in a hunt as a beater is sitting sweaty, catching his breath after a drive, when he sees a shadowy figure in a bush. He realises it is the White Lady, bows, and sees her kick a tree three times with her foot, looking at him sharply and nodding kindly. That evening at home he takes a spade, goes back to the spot where he saw the figure, and digs up a large chest. He prises the lid off with the spade, sees it is full of gold coins, and from then on he and his wife are free of poverty.
22532: A castle of the Knights Templar is said to have stood in the Rondeel, and seers such as Olden H. see the shades of the murdered knights floating there in their long white cloaks.
22553: Every evening around nine Jan stops playing cards and leaves. His parents, with whom he plays, find this strange, and his mother tells the priest, who sends the chaplain to play along (instead of the neighbour). When Jan wants to leave, the chaplain asks him to play a little longer and he agrees to a few more rounds. Then he really wants to go, and the chaplain puts his hand on Jan's shoulder (and presses him down). Jan begins to sweat while another round is played. Then it is half past ten, and with a crash a black skin falls down the chimney into the fire. The chaplain orders the mother to slide the hearth door shut in front of it, while he himself holds Jan. A smell of burning fills the house. Then Jan throws his arms around the chaplain's neck and says: "Thank you, you have saved me; I am rid of it; I don't have to go any more."
22574: A man tries to catch a rabbit, but it keeps jumping away. When the rabbit seems to be cornered, the man throws his club at it, but then he sees a calf walking in the meadow.
22582: A girl was courting a boy and often went out with him. Once they drove off in a carriage. On the way the boy said: "I have to get out for a moment." He climbed out of the carriage. A little later a wolf came and wanted to attack the girl, but went away again. The boy came back and the girl told him what she had seen. They drove on together and went into an inn. Then the girl was startled, because she saw that the boy had a thread from her petticoat between his teeth. The wolf had bitten into it. That boy could turn into a werewolf.
22585: Boiling the urine of a sick child thought to be bewitched, to make the witch come into the house and punish her.
22589: Besseme Garteje is suspected of witchcraft, so nobody wants to associate with her. Once she stepped into a maid's new clogs and left her old ones in their place. Once she is sitting in the bushes beside the Landeweer and is spied on. They see her make mice, but they have no tails.
22591: In the old days it was haunted everywhere. Also when you went to Elten by the back way. People always saw something in the woods there. And they did not dare go through there even in broad daylight.
22592: A poacher always sees an animal as big as a sheep walking in the woods, but when he wants to shoot it, his gun does not go off.
22593: One evening a man sees a hearse with mourners coming towards him, walks straight at it, but is flung squarely aside. The hearse came from this neighbourhood, and not six weeks later there was a funeral in this corner.
22596: A farmhand coming from the meadow meets a foal halfway, a werewolf. He has a sharp knife in his pocket, but goes back to take another road; again he meets the foal and takes a third road. Again he meets the foal and says: "Go away or I'll cut you across the muzzle." The foal comes at him and he gives it a big cut across the snout. At once it changes into a person he knows well.
22597: A farmer has 3 farmhands; 1 wants to go out every evening, and one night the other 2 follow him. They see him take a belt out of a willow, put it on and run off as a foal, and they know: he is a werewolf. They want the farmer to get rid of him. The farmer goes to the priest, who advises him to boil the belt under guard, which the farmer does; and although the farmhand is far away on an errand, he is suddenly there and has to be held back by 7 men until the belt has boiled away and he is freed.
22602: As a man and a woman unfasten the gate of his yard, a dead man appears to them; he vanishes once they are on their own yard.
22604: One evening a woman, Bartje, is keeping watch with the gun and wants to shoot a hare, but a large grey cat chases the hare away. Then she shoots at the cat, and the next day a well-known witch lay in bed with shot in her backside.
22613: When father has to fetch the midwife one evening, he passes a haunted farmyard, sees the ghost standing there and greets it. Later he goes to the priest, who contacts Father Grarus in Babberik, who comes and gives the ghost a place in the cellar where it used to live. They bricked that place up with a wall.
22614: Mother went to the well one evening and said: "Come here a moment and look at those little lights going up into the sky over there." I asked: "What does that mean?" She had heard from her parents that they were will-o'-the-wisps, innocent children who had not been baptised; they wandered between heaven and earth.
22617: The neighbour woman, a crossing keeper, always closes the railway barriers at 12 o'clock at night. Once, while reading the newspaper, she heard the barriers come loose, went to look at once and saw a black hearse with people behind it. But it was gone at once. A few days later a corpse from the neighbourhood passed by; so she had had a premonition, a second sight.
22618: A neighbour's child was seriously ill after eating a witch's apple (or something like that). The mother went to Father Grarus in Babberik, who advised her to open the feather pillow. There turned out to be a wreath in it, so finely woven that no human could have done it better. The witch was invited and came, but the mother had received a relic from Father Grarus which she had to put under the chair. Then the witch could not leave. They stoked up the fire and her husband put some more logs on. The witch wanted to leave but had to stay seated. Then they took the wreath and the man said: "So, witch, now we've got you." They threw the wreath into the fire and it flew up the chimney. The witch simply stood up and said: "A thousand thanks, man, for saving me, because now I am rid of that misery."
22623: A man cycling at ten Bos at midnight sees a ghost dog the size of a calf. Some say it was his own shadow, but others have seen it too.
22626: A group of six farmers always played cards until about ten o'clock, except one, who left at nine. Once they decided to follow him and saw him go to an old pollard willow, put on a bearskin and go off. Later he came back and changed (in the tree). They thought: "Something's not right with that fellow; he's up to something." The farmers decided to send him far away with a sand cart to Nijmegen, took the bearskin out of the tree and burned it on a big fire. But when it was almost burned, the farmer came back on horseback (he had left the cart behind), but he was too late; the skin was burned. Then he said: "Lads, you were lucky it got burned, because otherwise I would have destroyed you all."
22629: A man is pursued by 7 phantom animals (wolves) that bang violently against the front door.
22630: A traveller from Germany saw a man with a very broad hand in the woods of the Parkes and said: "Good evening." The ghost waved its hand and climbed a tree.
22631: A man returning on Saturday evening from his work in Germany sees a wire stretched across the road in the Parkes and steps over it, a little later another one, and another, and so on all the way to his house. There he hears noise behind the house, goes to look, hears it in front, then behind again, etc. He asks the priest for advice, who tells him to hold a novena. On the ninth day the priest blesses the house and the land. The ghost then ends up in a little box in the cupboard, which the priest takes away and bricks up between two walls.
22635: Someone is followed by a large dog and throws a stone at it, but the dog keeps following him to his house, and then turns into a man.
22636: In de Vianen a woman in white clothes floating above the ground was sometimes seen at night.
22640: Apparition of an old Juffer (lady), a shade.
22641: A farmer who falls asleep in front of his house and wakes at 11 o'clock hears and sees a hearse approaching, which stops behind the neighbour's house. Later this happens exactly the same way; so he had had second sight.
22645: Every evening a man is chased all the way to his door by a little white dog with red eyes that does not bark.
22652: A man is frightened by a big dog (constipation from the consternation).
22654: A man who sees a bundle of hay on the road one evening kicks it and is dragged into the air, slammed down on the "Bargse Heuf" and gets home very late.
22655: A neighbour picked up a pigeon from the road and looked at it, and the pigeon knocked all the teeth out of his mouth with its wings.
22657: A crusader returns as a ghost to his wife's tournament, wins her, reveals himself at midnight and sinks into the ground with her.
22658: Late in the evening a man has to fetch paraffin in a beer bottle, sees a werewolf on the path and hits it on the head with the bottle. In the morning he sees that the other farmhand has a badly battered head. He is now freed from that prank (going about as a werewolf).
22659: At night the narrator saw a few fireballs rolling across the road, and a little later a calf with glowing eyes was lying in the middle of the road.
22660: The little son of the narrator's brother is ill. On a neighbour's advice, Door takes the child to the fathers in Babberik, but on her return grandmother Door is advised by the neighbour woman to open the pillow; there is an almost closed wreath (of feathers) in it. The narrator advises his brother to boil the wreath; then the person who did this to the child will come. That person comes and lifts the pan off the stove.
22662: At night in the churchyard the narrator sees a headless man come out of a grave, greets him, gets no answer, and after a breath of wind the ghost is gone.
22663: A man gleaning ears of grain late in the evening sees a chestnut horse with a cart and a white and a black fellow loading rye. But when he checks in the morning, nothing is missing and nothing is to be seen.
22664: A cyclist finds his way blocked in the evening by two ladies in white with horses and has to turn back (later he fell ill).
22665: A farmer sees a strange cat at the milk and hits it on the head with a piece of wood; the cat runs off to where a witch lives; the next day she has a big hole in her head.
22666: When a farmer burns the wood of a pollard willow on which the witch once sat, it hisses as if there were snakes inside; so he gives it to his neighbour.
22668: On a farm there was a devil in the shape of a dog. It made strange leaps and walked on the beams. The fathers from Babberik were called. Two fathers come, draw a circle on the ground with a cross in it and call the dog, seize it, and the dog grows smaller and smaller until it fits into a matchbox, with which they leave by the ferry and bury it at Babberik in the monastery garden together with a cup and a bucket without a bottom, so that it will have work forever.
22672:
The narrator's sister is ill, the goats are ill; the fathers of Babberik and Huizen say you should not believe in witchcraft. Her godfather advises a novena to Sittard.
The neighbour woman, a witch, stole the butter. On someone's advice the mother boils the milk in a pot with holy water; it does not boil over and a bubble forms on it, which the mother stabs with a knife. At the same moment the cat that had come in during the boiling attacks the house cat. The witch does not come by the next day, but every year a willow dies.
22673: A farmhand is scolded by the farmer because the manure has not yet been spread; he says he is possessed by the devil, who spreads the manure for him. Within five minutes it is done.
22674: Mother often saw little lights behind the Zeddam mill, a sign that there is money buried in the ground there.
22675: A woman sees a white figure on the road, with a clergyman beside it to move passers-by aside.
24617: A phantom animal once seized a young man. The animal is as big as a two-year-old pig. It has bluish skin like an elephant, a crooked head, a long tail with a tuft, round claws and cloven toes.
29922: Voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of misfortune are howling dogs, magpies on the roof, black cats, and hens that come out of the barn or threshing floor with crossed straws on their backs.
30295: A sick horse has been bewitched by the devil. To keep the devil away from the horse, men sit by the animal at night waving a sharp knife.
31745: On certain days, if you look over the shoulder of a woman born with a caul, you can see into the future.
32021: When no butter forms during churning, witchcraft is at work. A devil-banisher once advised putting a hot poker into the sour milk. After that the milk still turned into butter.
32022: A strange red cat jumps at hanging bacon and gets a hard blow with a poker. The next day a woman - a witch - walks about with a cloth over her eye. This witch had changed into a red cat the day before.
32023: A light is always visible at a certain spot. It is an omen: later a wijk (canal) is dug at that spot.
34657: The cows of a man from Koekange are being milked, and one morning a neighbour sees a woman milking from a rus (clump of rushes), who begs him not to give her away.
34659: Screeching and whistling, once taken for the 'scheuvelloper' (skater) in the sky, is afterwards seen as a prediction of the train.
34666: On the Kuipersdijk a headless foal haunts at night.
34737: If a dog sits down by a house and howls, someone there will die; likewise if many magpies fly around the house.
34862: Everyone in the village was afraid of an 80-year-old woman who could do magic (an apple received from her turned into a toad). Only Jan Japiks' wife Engel, a name given to her by the schoolmaster who had adopted her as a foundling, was wiser, laughed at it and helped the old woman. But when Engel falls ill she cannot help the woman, who visits her, but is seen by someone who tells Jan. He is then convinced his wife is bewitched, and with a band of neighbours he goes to the old woman's house and shouts at her to lift the spell from his wife. The others see that the woman is ill, even dying, and leave, and the woman confesses to Jan that Engel is her child, and then dies.
34864:
A family with five children gets five apples from the neighbour woman. The mother says the apples must be kept until the next day, but the youngest son secretly takes a bite out of two of the apples at night. The next evening they want to eat the apples, but then it turns out that all five apples have turned into toads, and that two of the toads are missing a piece of their heads.
A young man goes to a witch's to have coffee and cake. At night he falls ill. The smith advises him to put away a jug in the dark, which the witch must not see. The boy follows the advice and recovers.
34865: If a child is born with a caul, the parents must burn the caul as soon as possible. If they do not, the child will be unhappy. Someone who owns such a caul is glad of it in wartime, because the caul makes its owner invulnerable and bulletproof. People born with a caul can see a funeral procession coming in advance. They must then go to the churchyard on the evening before the funeral to bring the corpse there ahead of time. One day a farmhand born with a caul goes to watch a funeral procession. A younger farmhand wants to come and watch, but the older one warns him he will not see anything anyway. When the younger farmhand complains that he indeed sees nothing, he gets a blow to the head. From that moment the young farmhand has the caul and the older one is free of it.
34975: A father and son live in a hole under the ground. To rob and murder passers-by, they stretch a rope with a bell across the road so they can hear passers-by. One day a girl comes by. The son does not want to kill her because he wants her as his wife. For a year father and son never leave the girl alone, but after a year they have to go out together after all. The girl manages to escape. The son runs after her and throws an axe at her, but he misses. The girl tells the schout (sheriff) everything, and the two murderers are beheaded. At the spot where the two murdered so many people, the victims still haunt as witte wieven (white women).
34976: A girl who was cutting rye was kidnapped by Ellert and has to shave his father Brannert every day; she cuts his neck, etc. The axe thrown after her lands in the threshold, where it can still be seen.
34977: The kidnapped girl is left alone after a year and then runs off. Eldert almost catches up with her and throws his axe, but only hits the door.
35055: A hunter always misses a certain hare and is advised by the baron to put 3 grains of rye in his shot charge. This time he hits the hare, but it runs off. Then the neighbour woman turns out to be lying in bed with her head wrapped in cloths. She recovers, but the hare is never seen again.
35267: The narrator's parents can fix people to the spot, even in advance. Reciting spells with which unwanted persons are fixed to the spot and released. The gift can only pass from a man to a woman or from a woman to a man.
37286: Someone known for his boozing, swearing and mocking was once found with his head twisted round. He had been thrown three metres over the ditch. That had been the work of the devil.
37291: Roelfs Jaantje was a witch. She always sat at the window and when children passed she gave them an apple, but you were not allowed to eat it. Some children kept the apples, and later spiders turned out to come out of them, or a live toad.
37293: A child lying in bed in pain is being pricked by witches by means of a little doll. A witch who has turned into a cat cannot be shot; otherwise, if she is hit, she walks around the next day with her hand in a cloth.
37298: With the jack of spades you can make a bottle of drink come. The person who sends the card away must not be the same one who takes the bottle with the card attached. The bottle may also not hover above the table more than three times. By then it must have been taken. Otherwise strange things happen. The first glass of drink must be thrown over the left shoulder.
37986: My mother did not need to be taken home, because she always felt protected. On the way home a big dog came walking beside her, which disappeared when she opened the door.
37987: In the old days, when someone died, many dogs had been howling in front of the house a few days before.
37988: A man says that because dogs are howling eerily, someone will die. No one believes it, but it comes true.
37994: Father is suddenly lifted up and flung into the ditch.
37995: A young man who had been at the pub was chased by the devil on his way home.
39407: Various superstitions, including signs that foretell misfortune, death or (bad) weather.
39429: A witch looks back if you place your footstep crosswise over hers.
40540: If you are afraid of witte wieven (white women), you should drink beer. A farmer once did so. Even so they still tried to stop him, and almost jumped onto his horse.
40622: A boy goes to his neighbour because he has to write about old customs and haunting for school. The neighbour tells several stories. First he tells about the various customs surrounding funerals. Then about the sighting of a black ghost. There was also a ghost hare that could not be hit, but when it was finally hit with a silver dime, it turned out to be an old witch. When the butter would not churn, a black hen was boiled alive, after which the witch came to lift the spell. A boy wants to steal a golden cup from the witte wieven (white women), but is chased, and his horse loses its tail. Another boy throws a spit at the witte wieven (white women), and he too escapes, but not without his horse losing its tail. Witte wieven (white women) could sometimes also be helpful and then did work on the land at night.
40914: A man knows he is guilty after assaulting a girl and then murdering her, but reassures himself by thinking that only God and the Devil know. The Devil appears and points to a rope with a noose hanging from a tree. He knows he has no choice but to hang himself. He is buried on the same spot.
41135: A dog is restless for a few days before the death and calms down afterwards, but the narrator does not believe that the howling of dogs is a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of death.
41141: A woman was not born with a caul, but hears in advance sounds connected to events that happen later.
41142: A man who can see events in advance advises someone to insure his house, because he has seen it on fire.
41143: A howling dog is voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a death, because it is no longer seen after a death in the family.
41144: A man who can see the future knows which horses of which colour will pull a hearse.
41145: A family very often sees something standing briefly against the wall. After a child dies, the coffin is deliberately not placed at that spot, but the bearer puts the coffin down at the place where something had been seen beforehand.
41146: Seeing a ship in advance at the place where a canal later comes.
41147: A family heard hammers knocking before the carpenter made the coffin in the house of the deceased.
41148: When a sheepfold is being built, it is said that the sound had already been heard beforehand.
41806: In one of his nicest articles in 't Nieuwsblad van 't Noorden, Tilbusscher lets an old woman speak: Witte Wijven (white women) were not ugly and were dressed in snow-white. They were mad about men. In Waarvem they often gathered. They danced around a thick tree. They waved white cloths with bloodstains on them. In Slochter they walked alongside people. They did nobody any harm. On the Wedder Brug they danced and sang.
42170: In the area there are witte wievenkoelen (white women's pits)!
42172: In the polder, the sounds of the midwinter horn seemed like ghosts.
42296: In Westerbroek witte wijven (white women) liked to dance around a tree in the woods at night. There was one widde juvver (white lady) whose gown was too long, so everyone tripped over it. A ziever cut it off, and from then on things always went well for him and his family.
42300: Sokkeraaiwiefkes (a kind of white women) do nobody any harm, but they do bring misfortune.
42312: Hiplichtjes (will-o'-the-wisps) always wander about and never find rest. Some were murdered and never had a burial; others are themselves to blame.
42313: A smakhak (ghost that throws itself down) haunts the Delleweg. It makes thudding sounds and slides past you. After the third time it goes away. It looks like a white dog.
42314: In Groningen many people believed in veurlopen (omens). In Middelsom a woman saw a hearse stop in front of her house with a white horse and a black horse in front of it. A white horse was never used for a hearse. A little later the woman died. When she was carried in the hearse, one of the horses fell into the ditch and was replaced by a white horse. Her prediction came true.
42324: An innkeeper sees a funeral procession pass by. Shortly afterwards the plague breaks out.
42327: Someone sees a funeral procession pass by. He also sees himself walking behind it. Later his brother dies. When a funeral procession comes by, you must always stay at the side of the road.
42329:
A man walked past a farm and heard people koekslaan (beating flax). He walked on and saw a barn on fire. When he came closer, it was gone.
Three weeks later it was Bouldag and two weeks after that the barn burned down.
42330: A man calls out to an empty horse and cart to halt. The horses stop. You should not walk along the side of the road at night, for then the hearse will drive you into the ditch. But do not walk in the middle of the road either, for then you will end up under it.
42335:
In Oetland a ship sank near Zoltkamp. The inhabitants think only of the goods and forget to save the people. The carter still haunts the place.
Oetland has been flooded.
42374: Two boys discover that a fellow card player is the devil, because they see a horse's hoof under the table.
42400: Griet Koenes from Muntjeziel was in league with the devil. When she died, nobody wanted her in the churchyard. They decided to take her to the sea by horse and wagon. Since then Griet has been haunting and wants revenge. She is coming very slowly closer to Muntjeziel and will one day take her revenge there.
42412:
Störtenbeker wanted to become a pirate. He went to Geuchie Mechail, who haunted the North Sea. Together they made the sea unsafe. When Störtenbeker had captured someone, that person had to try to drink a beaker empty. If he failed, he was thrown overboard. Only one man ever succeeded. Störtenbeker also had a lucky bone under his arm that made him invincible. When the Hamburgers had captured him by a trick, they beheaded him. As had been agreed, the head was not reattached to his body. He walked away without his head, and every pirate he passed would be set free.
The Hamburgers then went looking for the treasure. It was in the ship's masts, which were hollow.
42499: The Swieneslop is an empty piece of land that is haunted. When farmers have to go there, they always take a wooden nail to chase the ghosts away. You had just better not go there.
42500:
A house in Muntendam was terribly haunted, but the master would not give in and kept living there. Until one day a ghost fell down the chimney. Then he tore down the whole house and rebuilt it facing the other way.
Someone said that the master had treated his wife so badly that she died of grief. So it was supposedly his own fault.
42741: A dog starts howling before deaths, and lies down on the spot where the carpenter later puts a coffin.
42742: A dog jumping against the back door of a house where someone has died is an omen that the coffin will go out through the back door. A man tries to prevent this by locking the back door, but while he is digging the grave the coffin goes out through the back door after all.
42767: At the spot where men see a blue flame in the field one evening, to someone else a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a death, a shepherd later dies.
42771: A prediction that a house will be built on a certain spot comes true after the house that was built elsewhere burns down
42866: Men who have been frightened with ghost stories meet something black with glowing eyes on the road, which quickly disappears again. A man believes he met the devil in the shape of an animal. After he recites a psalm verse, the animal disappears.
42963: The nightmare is caused by a sorcerer. A farmhand keeps watch at night with a knife and hits something, and the next day the sorcerer has a cut across his face.
42965: Man sees a house on fire and feels that the walls are warm, an omen that the house will burn down.
42966: A little light is seen as a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the building of a farm.
42967: Urgent advice to take out fire insurance, because someone has seen the house on fire. Some time later the house burns down.
42971: A man tells the minister he has seen a hearse coming from a farm where bachelors live, and how a woman and a child fell out of the coffin. The minister tells him to keep quiet. Later the new maid becomes pregnant, dies with her child, and both are taken to her village in one coffin.
42991: A tramp sometimes sees ghosts, after which a farmer chases them off by swinging an axe.
42992: Seeing a ship sail at the place where a canal later comes; do not walk in the middle of the road, or you may be pushed aside.
43001: Where little lights used to dance in a row, there is now a road where bicycle lamps travel in a row one behind the other.
43002: Hearing the knocking of hammers and the ticking of a watch turns out to be a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the building of houses.
43011: Sometimes wood for the coffin lies ready in advance; sometimes hammering is heard in that wood.
43012: A man sees funerals in advance.
43014: A man is followed by something, stops and thinks it is the devil.
43018:
Living conditions in the peat region; storytelling evenings with ghosts and witches, among other things.
Anecdote about a woman who thinks the dog must also become a soldier.
A woman locks the door and the children must stay inside when she sees a suspected witch. Warning that an apple from the witch can turn into a toad or frog, and if she comes near a cradle she can bewitch the child.
43020: A warning not to walk in the middle of the road, or you risk being flung aside. Children never walk in the track of a hearse.
43085: A child has fallen ill after a witch looked at it. A man kicks a yellow cat; the next day the woman regarded as a witch has scratches on her head.
43087: Before there is a road, the sound of a dog cart and the barking of dogs is heard.
43088: Before a house is built, the sound of roof tiles sliding over the roof is heard.
43089: Hearing and seeing a steam train before there is any talk of a train running there.
43091: A man sees funeral processions; others see lights where roads are later built.
43098: A family puts a separate window in the house, so that the man who has to get up at night because he sees a funeral procession can stay inside.
43101: A priest's attempt to drive a ghost off a farm with a consecrated belt fails. The ghost is driven out through a hole in the wall, which is closed up at once.
43102: A carter sees that the man he has given a lift has a horse's foot. The next man who gets a lift says he knows who is sitting on the wagon, and explains how to get the ghost off the wagon.
43106: When Engel Pompkeblad sleeps, he does not breathe. He wakes up after a white mouse has jumped into his mouth.
43108: Witte wieven (white women) are spirits, actually little worms, on the heath.
43109: Howling dogs and the screeching of magpies are voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of deaths.
43115: A skipper believes his dead wife comes back in the shape of a cat.
43116: Fear of the churchyard; claim that white figures come from the churchyard.
43117: A woman predicts a fire and exemption by lot from military service; she sees a man go through a gate and vanish, while she herself has to open the gate.
43118: The rattling of a coach and the tread of horses is heard on a sand road where a brick road is later laid.
43119: A man warns people to step aside for a hearse that cannot be seen.
43120: The hearse a man sees turns out to be an omen of his own funeral.
43121: People saw a haunted house on fire, but it was demolished instead of burned down.
43122: The belief that crows and magpies screeching around a house are an omen of a death.
43124: A sorcerer falls asleep and only wakes up when a mouse jumps into his open mouth.
43128: A man grabs a girl and throws his arms around her, but his arms pass right through her, and the girl vanishes.
43129: The devil tangles the horse's mane at night.
43130: Boys do not steal apples and bread from someone who is reputed to be able to fix people to the spot.
43132: After the churn is bewitched, the milk cannot turn into butter.
43133: At night a boy sees his own family's brown horse and grey horse in front of a hearse, and a funeral procession from which one person is missing. When this man dies, the boy tells what he has seen. No one believes him, but all the horses refuse to pull, except the brown one and the grey one.
43134: After a bang is heard, nothing is seen outside. Later the same bang is heard and it turns out the tram has derailed.
43135: Magpies on the windowsill foretell that a death will occur in that house, for the narrator has experienced it himself.
43136: Haunting on a farm after the farmer has removed the little fence around his wife's grave. Once the fence is back, the haunting stops.
43137: Haunting around a house when no watch is kept stops when bales of straw are placed in front of the door.
43138: At night there is knocking on the window, but nothing can be seen. Later, at night, there is again tapping on the same window, by men bringing the news that their son is dead.
43139: A man born with a caul sees funeral processions, and sees a ship sailing over land where a canal was later dug.
43141: For the first three years storks throw something out of the nest. Under their wings sit bouwmannetjes (little builder men). Whoever sees a bouwmannetje (little builder man) for the first time without much money will have little money the whole year.
43142: Examples of voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a death: a mole burrowing under a path, chairs sliding through the room at night and cups and saucers rattling.
43143: A woman who is accused of keeping a child sick strokes the child, after which it dies. After being accused of being the reason the child could not die, she takes revenge by making cattle sick.
43144: A woman sees a hearse at the neighbours' that suddenly vanishes. At a later death a hearse stands in the same spot.
43145: A warning to a boy not to go along with someone who gets up at night, for example to see a funeral. The other will make him look over his right shoulder to pass on the gift and be rid of it himself.
43146: A group of card players wanting to go home ignore a warning that they cannot cross the bridge. They come back because a figure has blocked the bridge. After the master assures them nothing will happen to them, they can cross the bridge.
43147: Card players do not trust a black cat; it is said to be the woman known as a witch. The cat gets a blow on the head; the next day the neighbour woman has a head wound.
43150: Examples of voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event): a horse refuses to go on because a hearse is coming; seeing a coffin carried in, later a death; a dog howls at a sick man's house; misted-up windows mean disaster; being lifted up and picked up while walking on the road.
43151: Warnings about witches: do not accept an apple; lights in the field are witches; a wreath in a pillow comes from bewitchment.
43157: People who return after their death.
43158: Belief in ghosts; do not kick them but avoid them; ghosts bite children's legs.
43160: A witch has bewitched the churn and the milk cannot turn into butter.
43162: Howling of dogs and screeching of magpies is an omen of a death.

43261: A woman regarded as a witch can change into a cat; when that cat was struck, the woman walked about the next day with a cloth around her head.

43265: A crow on the mast foretells misfortune, but a woman's thought that her father will soon die does not come true.

43279:

43281: A man sees a funeral procession; the boys do step aside, but still get pushed.

43289: A little light is seen above a canal at the spot where a child later drowns.
43290: A prediction comes true that the horse pulling the hearse refuses to cross a bridge.

43294: General feeling that the howling of a dog, the screeching of a magpie and the hooting of an owl are omens of misfortune.
43296: Voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a funeral: seeing the course of a funeral beforehand.
43297: A farmer is thrown aside while ploughing; a few years later the plough breaks at that spot.
43298: A man who has to go at night to places where something happens says that only his spirit sets out, while his body stays at home.
43300: A witch makes mice dance when she is drunk.

Anecdote about a man who believes a female collector of folktales was sent by the devil.
The devil sits among water-lily leaves, lures people there and pushes them under water.
43306: The bubbling of water under a bridge is attributed to a witch pumping there.
43310: A white figure disappears when spoken to. It is supposed that she was the voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a woman who now lives on that road.
43311: Men see a fire at a spot; one of them predicts that a house will one day be built there.
43312: A man thinks he is being chased by the devil, dives into the box bed at home and thinks he sees the devil there too.
43313: A man sees a funeral procession in which one of the horses is unknown to him. At the funeral it turns out that one of the farmers has bought a different horse.
43315: No belief in witchcraft; belief that the screeching of a magpie and the howling of a dog were voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a death.
43318: Men lying in wait for friars are fixed to the spot by the friars, and can only go on when the friars bless them.
43319: Men see the mill house burning in advance, with the smoke going against the wind. Later the mill burns down, with the smoke going in the same direction as seen before.
43326: Circumstances of storytelling, older people telling stories to frighten people; causes of the decline of belief in ghosts.
43340: Haunted house; a sinful man fears a crucifix and returns after his death.
43341: A black sheep is mistaken for the devil in the dark.
43342: A farmer who takes land for himself while ploughing is trodden on the heels by the devil as a warning.
43343: Examples of voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event): seeing flames predicts misfortune; a light above water meant a drowning; howling dogs and magpies mean a death.

43357: Men see a fire, but the next day nothing is wrong with the house; a few years later there is indeed a fire.
43358: A woman who sees funeral processions at night has to get up.
43359: Walking in cart tracks brings bad luck.
43362: General belief that the howling of a dog and the cawing of a magpie are an omen of a death.

43395: A maid living with two wicked men stabs one of the men to death and flees. The other man pursues her and, just as she shuts the stable door, throws an axe after her. The axe was fixed in the stable door of a new farmhouse as a reminder.
43396: Examples of witches, the devil, voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event).
43401: Examples of voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event): where little lights were seen, roads with cars and bicycles later run; seeing fires in advance.
43403: Warning to children not to follow will-o'-the-wisps. Dishonest land surveyor returns after his death.
43404: By thinking of a person and sticking pins into the head, belly or legs of a doll, someone can be harmed.
43407: A stranger is allowed to join a card game; after they notice something strange about him, they leave. After they have gone, the café owner is beaten; one of the card players drowns.
43409: Man says he foresaw someone's death, and says he saw a house on fire, but the house is still standing.
43410: Seeing in advance a ship with a sail and a white horse in the field where a canal was later dug.
43412: The howling of a dog and a magpie pecking at the window are omens of a death.
43413: A man who can foresee evil sees little fellows walking on the roof of a house. Later he sees a little man waving on the roof and a fireball when the waving stops. Later the house burns down.
43415: A man believes that meeting a black cat or someone with a hunchback brings bad luck.
43417: Howling dogs that jump up, magpies and church bells that sound duller mean a death.
43433: A week after a woman has watched a hearse drive by for several minutes, a real hearse passes there.
43434: Fog smells like smoke, with the thought that there will soon be a fire. Others see fires in advance, and can feel at the door latch whether a fire or a death is coming.
43465: Some people lie awake at night and lie dead still; they are then troubled by the mare.
43466: A woman who walks the streets one night because she has seen her dead husband hangs herself the next night.
43469: A red sky is seen as an omen of war.
43473: On the way to an illegal bar a man meets a black phantom dog, which, when asked what it is going to do, answers that it is going to fetch a bottle of jenever (Dutch gin).
43477: The narrator meets a foal at night, thinks it is a phantom animal and kicks it. The next morning a farmer has a lame foal.
43481: If all the feathers in a sick person's pillow have been woven together into a wreath, the sick person dies.
43483: Examples of deaths after howling dogs were heard. People believe that a black dog that comes into the house is a returning dead person; they believe that after the priest blesses the house the dead person will not return.
43495: Predicting the building of a tramline after seeing a row of lights, the building of houses, and the digging of a canal after seeing ships sailing at that spot; predicting that money will become worthless; people who are murdered or die in accidents remain floating in the air.
43510: Children are afraid of a woman who can do magic. Apples she puts in a pillow turn a strange colour, and she can fly on a broom.
43512: People do not dare pass the house of a woman who can do magic and receives visits from freemasons.
43513: Fear of strangers near the cattle, of a cross in front of the house, and of witches coming in.
43514: A woman who can work magic holds the horses of the barge towers fast.
43515: Warning against a child being bewitched by a stranger; a pram tips over when a black dog walks alongside; a neighbour bewitches the churn, for she is wounded by a pitchfork that was placed tines first in the drain hole.
43519: A man born with a caul predicts the digging of a canal, the sailing of ships and the building of houses, sees white figures that disappear after he recites a psalm verse, sees a coffin standing on the road and predicts a funeral procession. 43521: A place was said to be haunted at night by a white horse, but someone who went to look with a revolver saw nothing.
43522: People's fear of a black cat.
43523: A man sees funeral processions and foresees deaths.
43524: On the road a black crow flies ahead of the horse and cart; in the storage, among the merchandise, is a mourning letter for the merchant's sister. The bird then flies away.
43526: Crows and magpies around the house announce a death.
43537: Contrary to custom, a shipyard boss forbids children to be on a ship being launched. A sorcerer predicts that the ship will then not move. When the children are let onto the ship, it slides straight down the slipway.
43545: Where a tram line later runs, people earlier see carts without horses at night that still move forward.
43548: Sometimes ghosts, which are mostly white, are seen on the road.
43549: A bird on the pitchfork can mean a death.
43550: A man believes it is a bad omen when all the lines on a ship are stuck, and sees the later storm in which everything on deck is washed away as the result.
43556: Advice to put a rosary on the pillow against dauwworm (ringworm); walking in cart tracks attracts bad luck. A man looking through a window is struck by an invisible devil; five black fingers appear on his cheek.
43569: Stubbing your foot against a stone means a funeral.
43572: Prediction that something will happen by a canal; people with a light were seen crossing a road. Later a drowned boy was carried home along that path in the evening.
43576: Cries for help are heard long before people drown at that spot in a canal dug later.

43579: A man tells another, who sees nothing, to step aside because a funeral procession is coming. The other man can see the procession when he places a foot on the left foot of the one who can see it.
43580: A prediction that one day many soldiers would come with wagons without horses. When the Canadians arrive in 1945, someone remembers this.
43581: Before the canal is dug, a man sees a ship with a horse in front of it at that spot; he also hears a bell strike at the place where a house is later built.

43584: Before a child drowns in the canal, a dog sits howling at that spot and will not be chased away; afterwards the dog stays away.
43586: A girl born with a caul sees a hearse on the threshing floor and hears the sound of clogs. A few days later her deceased grandfather is brought to that house.
43587: A carter pulls over for a funeral procession that someone else does not see.
43588: Floating little lights are seen as a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of, among other things, the building of a house, the laying of a road, the digging of a canal.
43589: A girl believes that witches exist. She thinks that apples from a witch have toads inside them and make you ill.
43607: Seeing voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of war, the building of a railway and fires; seeing ghosts of the dead.
43611: Omens of a death are the howling of a dog, a magpie's nest near the house, or always having magpies around the house.
43612: Hearing bolts sliding and a side door opening and closing must have been a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the arrival of the doctor, who walks along the same path and goes through the same door as was heard.
43613: The narrator thinks that the little light and posts grandmother saw are a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the cars and the telephone poles.
43614: A horse standing in the feeding trough is said to have been a forewarning of a later fire.
43615: An indifferent man admits that something exists after a fire in which all the trees are scorched black, but a magpie's nest still has green leaves.
43616: Experience that a dog's howling is the harbinger of a death.
43618: An animal resembling a big black dog that jumps off the cart must have been the devil.
43620: At a haunted spot a man sees someone approaching who looks like his sister-in-law, and who runs off when he says her name. He chases her, but at a ditch the figure has vanished.
43621: A spookkijker (person who sees apparitions) hears the sound of crockery and a lamenting voice. Later, during a house move, there is a woman who laments what has happened to her.
43622: A man hears cow chains rattling, and later a cowshed is built; he sees a threshing machine being lifted over the hedge at night, because a hearse has to pass.
43645: Man can foresee things; how he foresaw something as a little boy.
43646: At home the narrator sees people lying by a gate; it is his son's motorcycle accident.
43647: Advice to the buyer of a cow not to keep the animal long because prices are falling.
43648: Narrator foresees that a cow will fall ill, recover, fall ill a third time, then not recover and be worth nothing.
43655: A sick woman who hears a dog howling sees it as a sign that she will die soon. Small dogs cannot see misfortune.
43656: A girl sees a dead person being carried out of a house and who walks in the procession. After a death in that house, the funeral procession is just as the girl saw it.
43657: In the years when both world wars begin, a man sees little snakes growing through the veins of tree leaves.
43659: Voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the building of a church: hearing organ music and the singing of hymns.
43660: A farmer who treats his workers badly finds no rest after his death and returns to the farm. A priest holds out his hand wrapped in a handkerchief. After the spirit grabs the handkerchief and disappears, the farmer is not seen again.
43667: Examples where a magpie, a screeching owl and a howling dog are omens of a death.
43681: People who believe that witte wieven (white women) do good rather than harm are often made fools of. Example of people who believe that witte wieven come at night to mow rye. On the advice of friends they put out food for the witte wieven, after which the friends go mowing at night.
43689: A man senses that the mayor has had an accident. He goes home, where he hears that the mayor has died in an accident.
43690: Unexplained phenomena in a haunted house that no longer occur after the house is rebuilt.
43691: A sick girl sees men in front of and inside the house and hears coffee being ground. That night the girl dies; she had foreseen her funeral, because drinking coffee is a custom at a funeral.
43694: A little black man who comes to a woman at midnight and disappears at one o'clock beats up a man who wants to help the woman.
43695: A drunk man stabs the devil with a knife, whereupon the devil throws the man over a ditch.
43698: A bumblebee flying into the throat of a sleeping woman, who then wakes up, means that she is a witch.
43700: A gravedigger in a red shirt is seen; a wagon is heard arriving at the house and leaving again; men carrying a coffin are seen; a funeral is seen with acquaintances in the procession, the people as small as matchsticks.
43701: Example of voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a fire, and dreams of a damaged parcel and a death that come true.
43703: The sound of rye being shovelled when there is no rye, and livestock that is restless but lies quietly in the stable when people go to look.
43706: Magpies and jays foretell a death.
43710: A black cat sitting in front of the house in the evening is suddenly inside; the parents think the cat is the devil. A black cat sitting on the cows keeps coming back. After the cat has been struck, an old woman has a bump on her head the next day.
43712: A pious man, at his third encounter with a headless man who does not return his greeting, thinks it is the devil. After saying a prayer he never sees a headless man again.
