43714: Screeching and creaking in front of the door with nothing to be seen. After the tram line is built, the tram stops in front of the house and makes the same sound.
43719: A man makes people unable to move by holding their wrist. Looking along his stick he sees white caps in the peat bog; later women wearing white caps work there.
43721: The man who fixes a farmer to the spot turns out to have fixed other people to the spot before.
43723: A man sees things in advance: someone will one day own four horses, a funeral going to a churchyard that is laid out later, the colour of the horse before the hearse, wagons without horses.
43726: On the Geselberg people were flogged to death; in the past witches and ghosts were great tormentors.
43786: Stories about witches flying through the air on broomsticks and witte wieven (white women) with glowing eyes frighten children and adults.
43787: In a haunted house, werkgeesten (work spirits) knock.
43789: Dogs that sit howling in front of a house for a long time are a harbinger of a death. Shooting the dog does not help; the sick person dies anyway.
43797: The chattering of magpies is an omen of a woman's death. The narrator wants nothing to do with the screeching of birds.
43799: A sound that is heard while nothing can be seen is a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the collapse of the back wall of a stable.
43807: A man hears a voice saying the brown one must step over. At a funeral the brown horse is told to step over the harness.
43814: Narrator has heard voices indicating that accidents, illness or other harm are to be expected.
43816: A carter hears his two horses talking, saying they will be sold if he keeps drinking, but he ignores the warning, after which he has to sell his wagon and horses.
43819: A woman twice hears knocking on the window while there is nothing to be seen. Later someone knocks on the window to say that the neighbours' boy has drowned.
43820: A man twice sees his house on fire when it is not really burning. Later the house burns down.
43823: A house that someone saw on fire is still standing.
43880: A man sees a funeral procession in advance.
43881: A man sees a white figure coming towards him over the water and thinks it was the devil.
43883: At midnight a man is visited by something with chains on its legs that sits on him, so that he can hardly breathe. His companion hears and feels something but sees nothing. When he swings a piece of wood around he hits something. After that the figure stays away.
43888: A woman hears noises; her husband does not believe her. When he keeps watch on the house, he sees nothing. He finds his wife still in bed; she complains that a thing has sat on her again so that she cannot get up. After they move, nothing more happens.
43889: A white kale stalk is a bad omen; it means a death.
43890: The mare is an evil spirit that sits on someone at night. Deliverance from the mare by praying in the evening.
43894: A boy sees a little black man at night, the mare, who disappears when the bed is made up again.

43914: The spirit of a deceased person stays away once his debt to the poor has been paid.
43916: The devil beats a woman after she has said that he did not shoot through a tree, but past it.
43917: In the evening a man hears sounds of work on both sides of the church, but nothing can be seen. Later the rectory on one side is torn down and a new rectory is built on the other side.
43918: A star that a man sees falling on his neighbour's house was an omen of her death.
43919: While cycling, with no one and nothing nearby, the bulb holder is pulled out of the rear light.
43920: A prediction that a star will appear in front of the moon does not come true. But a diamond shape appears in the sky with a snake in it that crawls out of the diamond and moves eastwards. 43921: In the evening the string is removed from the door latch, otherwise no butter can be made the next day.
43922: A warning to step aside for a cart with a coffin is voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a death.
43924: In a haunted house men in top hats walk to the back door. Later the coffin of the dead farmer's wife will not go through the front door, so it has to go through the back door.
43926: A man believes that a gate opening and closing by itself is the work of a witch.

43937: Berendina (Dine meu) predicted that trains would come, when they did not yet run.
43947: Long before there were engines, Berendina (Dine meu) predicted that ships without sails would sail to Groningen and back.
43948: A woman predicts that much blood will flow on a small flight of steps.
43949: Berendina (Dine meu) predicted that brass handles would appear on the front doors of a house on the Reitdiepskade.
43951: The devil was in the merry-go-round. If you got on the merry-go-round, you were seized by the devil.

In the Sterrebos in Groningen the voice of an innocently hanged boy can still be heard.

44017: A man born with a caul sees a coach without horses years before the tramway is built.
44019: To drive the devil out of someone, she takes their head between her hands and says a prayer.
44023: People born with a caul; a howling dog, seeing floating lights and a burning house are omens of a death; mocking the devil; being held fast by the devil, a way to get free.
44025: Person born with a caul; returning dead; witch's wreath in a pillow; foreseeing the digging of a canal and the place where a person drowns.
44048: A few days before a death, a woman hears magpies chattering around the house.
44049: A hole gives off light from far away; as soon as you reach the hole, there is nothing to be seen. A treasure of money is said to be hidden in the hole.
44050: A swearer who says he is not afraid of the devil either never again says he is not afraid of the devil after being beaten up by something that follows him.
44051: A man sees witte wieven (white women) in white cloaks floating over the heath; he is fooled into believing that someone can make his hens lay eggs bearing his name.

44080: A man who is said to have murdered his wife regularly sees her. She stands in the doorway so that he cannot get in.
44081: A person who lived a wicked life comes back as a floating ghost in a white cloak.
44086: An educated and distinguished woman warns not to leave Christmas decorations up until after New Year, or else someone will die.
44091: Knives lying crossed over each other predict a quarrel.
44092: A prediction that all the white houses will burn down comes true; only the white church is still standing.
44121: A parish priest fixes a robber to the spot; when he lets him go, the robber of course does not dare threaten him a second time.
44125: Fear of howling dogs and magpies. The narrator experiences a death after a dog has sat howling with its head raised.
44126: Lights are seen as a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of fire.
44128: After two owls that have sat screeching in front of a house are shot dead, two deaths occur in that house.
44129: A haunted house where knocking is heard in the evening; a black figure with a chain around its legs attacks a woman.
44132: A man who does not believe in ghosts and witches would like to see something for once. One night he suddenly stands in the middle of a bright light; a few weeks later, at the same place and the same time, but then in the afternoon, he meets a funeral. He also sees a fire that is not there.
44134: A prediction that someone will drown in a canal within a day comes true.
44135: A dead woman comes back when her child has to leave the house after her husband remarries. Once the child is back with the father, the woman's ghost stays away.
44136:
The narrator was born with a caul, so she knows many things in advance. Her caul was burned straight away, so she does not have to go out and look at night.
She sees lights at a place where a churchyard is later built.
44139: A doctor warns people to step aside because of an approaching funeral procession.
44140: Dogs howling as voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a death.
44142: A long line of churchgoers is seen as a funeral procession, and as an omen of a death.
44144: A man who earlier heard roof tiles sliding down hears the same sound when a house is demolished.
44145: On the spot where a woman hears the sound of rattling plates and spoons in plates, a house is later built.
44146: At the place where he lives a man hears water flowing, a portent of the lock chamber in the canal that was dug later.
44147: A girl says that the ghost of her dead father floats through the air, also around the house. In a haunted house one floorboard keeps coming loose.
44152: At primary school a story was played from a tape: a young nobleman oversleeps on Easter and misses the church service in Usquert. He demands that the minister start again. From then on dragons, hunting dogs and ghosts are seen at the site of the farm.
44200: In the 19th century the minister of the Kloosterkerk in Ten Boer walked every Saturday along the Damsterdiep to a fellow minister in a nearby village (Thesinge). 44201: The convent well in Ten Boer was not to be trusted. A nun who had become pregnant had drowned her child there. It was better not to go there in the evening. The well also never ran dry and was always full.
44210: When black crows sat together, it was said that someone would die. The pallbearers were also called black crows.
44215: Around 1880 there was the sect of the Holy Spirit in Zoutkamp; many members were descendants of the seeress Meldine.
44218: A man could not pay his bills. When the tax officials came by, he dressed up as a ghost and they left. The house was known as a haunted house with doors that opened by themselves.
44258: After a witch's visit there is a wreath in the pillow; the witch is injured when a dog has been kicked; apples she gave have turned into toads the next day.
44259: A man sees deaths in advance; the height of the people in the funeral procession determines the time of the funeral.
44260: Dogs howl and smell the odour of a corpse before a death.
44262: Seeing a ship with a cloth on a pole on land is a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a canal; something going along the road without a horse is a voorloop of the tram.
44263: Voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) was not regarded as anything special, and was believed.
44264: A mocker meets the devil as the fast mower.
44268: Cows that have run dry may be bewitched. After a bezetter (charmer) has bored little holes in their ears, the cows give milk again.
44270: With a bewitched churn, butter-making fails.
44271: A turtle dove in the house as protection against whooping cough and dauwworm (a skin rash).
44275: A dog that howls for several evenings is an omen of a death. After a child has drowned, the dog stops howling.
44276: A man is picked up by something and thrown into the water.
44278: Seeing a house burning when nothing is wrong with it is an omen of a death in that house.
44279: Nobody dares to cross a footbridge, because there is always a man standing there, possibly the devil.
44280: A carpenter warns his mother not to walk between two stacks of wood, because he has encountered something there. When he walks there himself, he is killed by sliding wood.
44281: When there is knocking in the wood for a coffin, nothing can be seen. Later a child drowns and the knocking stops.
44283: A funeral procession makes a man fall; dislike of magpies.
44290: Some people see funeral processions in advance; it is not known whether people are recognised or whether one has to get up at night.
44291: The screeching of a magpie predicts a death.
44292: To prevent the devil from coming to churn at night, which would mean no butter could be made the next day, the pin holding the beam of a churning mill must be removed in the evening.
44294: A man who has dealt with the devil is found dead with his head turned backwards on his body.
44300: The ghost of the notorious drost Rudolph de Mepsche haunts the castle for a long time.
44362: Perceiving events in advance: the clatter of horses, later horses bolt; seeing ships on the heath, where a canal is later dug; seeing a white figure, later a hearse gets stuck in the snow at the place where the ghost was seen.
44366: Whoever has money in their pocket when first hearing a wagtail or lark sing in spring will never be short of money. The reverse is also true, which is why children are given money in spring.
44367:
A woman who is thrown aside knows that a hearse will pass. 
A man who meets a funeral procession asks who is being carried away, and his own name is given.
44370: A man saw many people in Sunday clothes coming out of a barn. He had had a vision of the future: later a church was built there.
44373: A man watching a felled tree being hauled away fixes the horse to the spot so that it cannot go on. When the man leaves, the horse starts walking again.
44374: Witch cats hold a farmer's horse fast. When they leave, the horse starts walking again.
44380: A corpse that lies unburied over a Sunday means another death within six weeks.
44383: In a new house a woman feels someone walking behind her and hears her husband making coffins in advance. In another house the woman is not troubled.
44384: A coffin is seen on the threshing floor, which later turns out to be for the daughter. A friend bumps into something invisible; later a coffin is placed on that spot.
44385: Dogs howl at places where a death will occur and can hear the moaning of a sick person from a distance.
44386: A girl is bitten in the leg by a witch or the devil, after which she keeps getting smaller. After the priest tells her to pray the evil spirits away, she gets better.
44389: In Sellingen there is the wijvenbrug (women's bridge), named after the witte wieven (white women). People were afraid of the wisps (of mist) that drifted across the road from a low-lying piece of land near the bridge when there was lightning.
44393: A variegated kale plant among the green ones means a wedding in the family.
44395: Voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a birth: the midwife hears knocking on the window.
44410: Where a pub disappeared, a pool has formed where little lights burn, a head rises from the water and fireworks shoot up. A man shouts at the pool that it should just come out, and flees on hearing a voice saying something must be finished first before he comes. He has just got home when there is a crackling behind him and the back wall bursts apart.
44436: In the evening a man is joined by a small woman with long hair. Both stay silent. At home he sees a jet of fire shoot up into the sky.
44437: A ban on eating an apple received from a witch. The next day the apple is gone and there is a toad in the dish.
44439: Men can also learn witchcraft. Boys who have learned it pronounce the spell wrongly, so they do not fly over the wood but have to walk.
44464: Examples of the devil's work: fire on both sides of a path along which a man walks with his horse, a black thing rolling towards them; a hunchback walking in front of man and horse.
44467: A cat washing itself predicts visitors. A magpie on the windowsill that pecks and screeches is an omen of a death.
44468: The spirit of a dead person stays away if the door is set upside down in its frame, because then the latch cannot be found. This does not help if a promise has not been kept. As soon as the promise is fulfilled, the dead person is at peace.
44470: Women believe that roggemoeders (rye mothers, field spirits) are chasing them. A man on horseback lets them hold the horse by the mane and tail, so that they can escape.
44471: A farmer milking in the field feels something brush past him. Later a railway line is built.
44472: At a house where odd people always live there is a well above which, it is said, a little flame always burns.
44473: A charm as protection against a witch; hiding in bushes; turning apples into toads.
44484: The belief that a pinch in the calf that injures a boy is the devil's work. He is healed after the priest exorcises him.
44486: The milk will not turn to butter, so there must be a witch in the churn. On two attempts to put devil's dung under the threshold the man is thrown aside; the third time it works.
44491: A priest invites a man to ride in his carriage. When he discovers that the man has goat's legs, the priest says the man may stay seated if he has good intentions, but must leave if he is the devil. The man gets out, leaving a puddle behind.
44494: In [Klaziena?]veen, and also in Bellingwolde, stories were told about witte wieven (white women).
44503: At school they were told that a kind of ghost, a child snatcher, lived in the cornfield. When the narrator and his friends walked through the field, they saw something white. They were terrified, but it turned out to be a sheep.
44505: Some clairvoyant people saw a veurloop (foreshadowing), a carriage drawn by black horses. Someone would then die soon.
44506: When the dogs howled, someone would die.
44507: When someone died, two more had to follow. A triangle could always be drawn.
44509: Examples of voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of deaths.
44535: After walking three times around the cowshed with twigs of alder buckthorn and then three times around the churn, the churn yields butter again.
44537: Men see girls in white clothing rowing, who suddenly vanish. Later a child drowns at the place where the girls were seen.
44538: Braids in a horse's mane because the devil has ridden the horse at night.
44539: A man who sees nothing after being warned to step aside for a hearse is picked up and set aside.
44540: The call of an owl, a magpie on the windowsill and the howling of a dog predict a death.
44545: One evening a man meets a dog with stiff legs that will not move aside. He hits the dog and at the same moment falls unconscious. When he later comes to, there is nothing to be seen. The dog must have been the devil.
44546: A man who mocks the devil loses consciousness and dies the next day.
44547: A prediction that a farm under construction will never be finished proves right, because the farm burns down shortly afterwards.
44548: A grey cloth above the land is a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of ships in a canal that is being dug. A flame above the canal is a voorloop of a child drowning.
44550: A man walking on the higher part of the road is picked up and thrown down, because he has collided with a hearse.
44551: A warning not to accept an apple from certain women.
44552: In the evening a man hears cries for help from a thicket, but there is nothing to be seen. When the thicket is being cut down, a man gets caught on a branch, cries for help, falls to the ground and dies.
44554: A farmer sells his grey horse to his neighbour, because he predicts that the horse will take him to the churchyard. After the farmer dies, his own horses cannot be harnessed to the hearse. In the end the neighbour's grey is harnessed.
44556: A magpie as an omen of a death.
44557: When a boy falls ill, dogs appear that try to get into the house. After the sick boy has died, the dogs stay away. The narrator thinks he should not believe in it, but is glad he no longer hears dogs howling.
44558: A man who wants to convert his farm into a bakery sees the complete bakery standing there one evening. When he opens the door everything has vanished; later the bakery is built just as he saw it.
44559: When a man who can see things in advance has visited and does not come back, it means disaster.
44562: Hearing a turtle dove while there is no turtle dove in the house. The neighbours' turtle dove never calls, but does so when it is lodged with others while the neighbour's coffin is above ground. After returning to its owner, the turtle dove never coos again.
44563: As long as someone is ill, a dog howls near the house, but it is no longer seen after the sick person dies.
44564: Belief that magpies and starlings predict misfortune.
44565: As a joke, a doctor tells a farmer's wife who cannot get butter when churning that a certain woman must have bewitched the churn. He tells that woman she can fetch buttermilk from the farmer's wife. When the woman arrives at the farm she is told she has bewitched the churn.
44573: Ancestors keep silent about hiding a treasure, so their spirits have no rest and haunt at midnight. A farmhand addresses a spirit, which asks him whether he will carry out its task. As a pledge the farmhand holds out a pitchfork wrapped in a handkerchief to the spirit, which takes hold of it, leaving its handprint in the handkerchief. The spirit says a treasure is hidden in a wall. After the treasure is found, all stays quiet.
44576: A falling star above a house can be an omen that the house will burn down.
44577: Glow-worms predict the coming of a road with streetlights.
44578: A woman tells her daughter she has seen a light in a stack of peat. Later the body of the daughter's son is carried around a stack of peat.
44579: Grey horses bring bad luck and are never used to tow ships.
44580: A man who says the devil may finish the work believes that if the work is done after the weekend, the devil has done it.
44582: To avoid misfortune, boat-towers never use a white horse.
44583: Hearing knocking at night and seeing a row of people in top hats in front of a house is voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a funeral. People have to wait, because the coffin must go through the window. For that a window frame must first be removed.
44585: The devil chases someone and suddenly disappears.
44586: At midnight the ghost of a murdered person haunts and blood spatters up at the place of the murder. A boy then does not dare look over his right shoulder.
44610: According to the stories, the houses of the Jews deported in the Second World War were full of valuables. People searched under floors, in the garden or in the cellar, but the narrator never heard that anything was found.
44673: Baking pancakes fails; a woman sees a black cat sitting there which cries that the flour was stolen. The woman hits the cat on the head with the pan; the next day a woman known as a witch walks about with a bandage around her head.
44677: If the milk is bewitched, no butter forms in the churn.
44680: Witte wieven (white women) floating over the fields carry sand in their aprons and make hills.
44681: A death is coming when dogs howl and chickens walk around with a straw in their beak.
44707: Men who want to beat up a parish priest get no chance, because he fixes them to the spot and releases them when they promise to mend their ways.
44710: A farmer who moved a boundary stone has no rest after his death and asks where the stone should be put. When the wronged farmer answers that it must be put where it belongs, the voice disappears. The next day the boundary stone is in the right place.
44714: A man sees someone crawl out of the water with a bundle of straw. Later the man falls into the water and is saved when someone throws him bundles of straw.
44715: A prediction comes true that after a fatal accident, another dead person will be carried out of the same house after seven weeks; also, something else will happen after four weeks.
44716: The howling of dogs has meaning; why a dog does not approach a group of people; a dog sees a funeral procession in advance; preventing a dog from howling.
44719: Hauntings and second sight are imagination. Nobody dares steal fruit from a witch, but nothing happens to the narrator when he does.
44720: The remark that a woman who can do harm makes pigs sick is the reason such old women are seen as witches.
44721: Women meet a big dog that disappears when they say the devil must go away.
44722: Fear of a woman who learned witchcraft from her mother. Shaking up potatoes in a pan is a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the building of a house.
44723: Fixing people who want to steal peat to the spot.
44725: A dog howling in front of a house means something is going to happen. Prediction that a man with a brown horse will have a fatal accident.
44758: A neighbour takes pity on children who are not properly cared for by their stepmother. At night she knocks on the window and pretends to be the dead wife asking her husband about the children. The man believes his first wife has come back.
44759: Nobody dares to buy a house in which witte juffers (white ladies) walk.
44763: At night a woman hears someone go up to the attic, scoop grain into a sack there and come down. Later, after someone's death, she hears the same sound when rye is scooped for the bread for the funeral.
44777: A ghost or devil in a house grows smaller through the prayers of a friar and can thus be put in a little box. In a river floodplain the friar draws a circle and buries the box in the middle of it. People keep hearing ghostly sounds there.
44783: On the way back from fetching a kankerpop, a man is attacked by a werewolf, but he breaks its power by cutting it with a knife. After getting home he goes to the inn where he had been playing cards and finds the man who was the werewolf. The customers hold the man, and they see the skin burn in the hearth fire. The man is glad to be freed from having to go about as a werewolf.
44843: A man predicts a funeral and that the hearse bringing the deceased home will have to turn around.
44844:
In an underground dwelling on the Ellertsveld lived two giants, Ellert & Brammert. The place is barren because of a curse. Father Ellert and son Brammert robbed and plundered. To hear passers-by coming, they hung a rope with a little bell across the road. Thus near Orvelterveen they came upon a girl and carried her off. The girl had to stay in the robbers' den for seven years, but one day she murdered the father with a knife. Ellert ran after the woman and threw an axe at her, but it stuck in the door.
If you walk over the moorduil (murder hollow) at night, you can still see the ghosts of Ellert and Brammert. Their hands are smeared with blood, and at 1 o'clock at night they vanish again.
44855: A man believes that a wreath in his sick wife's pillow means the devil wants to kill her.
44858: A dead woman comes back and stays away once the debt she still owes has been paid.
44859: The mother of a pregnant girl abandoned by a young man hopes he breaks his neck. Later a horse bolts, the young man falls from the wagon and breaks his neck. A cross stands where it happened.
44861: When a woman wants to give a cup of water to an unknown man, the cup shatters, and at the same moment the man has vanished. One priest fails to drive the ghost away by praying, another succeeds. A cross stands at the place to which the ghost was prayed.
44866: Explanation of the name Meerland; Norsemen moor their ships to the church tower; drowned Norsemen float as ghosts over the water.
44868: After seeing a red flame over the roof, a man touches the door handle, which is cold. That means a death. A hot door handle would have meant that the house would burn down.
44869: After someone has been picked up and thrown aside on a haunted road, the driver of a threshing machine sometimes stops and makes the sign of the cross.
44903: Examples of curses that come true.
44908: In a beekeeper's house someone will die when the bees become restless.
44910: The giants Ellert and Brammert carry off a girl to work for them and serve as a wife. After seven years the girl Marieke manages to escape by cutting Brammert's throat. Ellert comes after her with his axe. The girl just manages to reach her parents' little farm in time. Ellert dies.
44914: Many villains went to Drenthe because in its wide open spaces they would not be caught. So the legend of Ellert & Brammert may contain a kernel of truth. The narrator's grandmother used to tell the story of Ellert & Brammert. They had taken Marieke of Orvelteveen to their den on the heath near Schoonoord. Marieke was chased, and an axe was hurled at her head. It stuck in the door. The stiepelteken (mark in the doorpost) was still visible in the ninth century in a house in Schoonoord. Marieke managed to escape by cutting the father's throat while shaving him. She also had a child by Ellert & Brammert, which was murdered.
44915: 'Grandpa Stavast' from the Brammershoopstraat in Eeserveen told the story of the giants Ellert & Brammert. According to Stavast, the giants' robbers' den was in Eeserveen. Marieke (the abducted girl) came from Oud Orvelte. A giant villain chased Mariek as far as Oud Orvelte. The giant threw an axe at the girl's head. The mark could be seen in the baander (barn doorway) for many years.
44918: The day after a black cat has been hit with a stick, a woman known as a witch walks about with a cloth around her arm.
44919: In a bewitched churn the butter will not come.
44920: A cart becomes harder and harder to pull because of a black dog in one of the wheels. The dog disappears when they stare hard at the animal. A room in a house whose door stands open every morning.
44921: Removing swallows' nests means someone will die; the cowshed should not be cleaned between Christmas and New Year; passing on bezetten (the power to bind or charm) usually stays in the family.
44924: Children make their dead mother come back; she declares that the remaining money must go to the poor, and disappears.
44926: When a man turns out to have a horse's hoof, everyone leaves.
44929: A woman sees the devil in a black form.
44931: A clergyman can drive away witches and devils by praying; every year they come a cock's step closer again.
44935: In the evening an alf (elf) is seen swimming in the canal.
44936: To banish the devil in the form of a cat, a priest reads from a book he takes out of a trunk. The devil falls down and is locked in the trunk, which is so heavy that the horses can barely pull the coach.
44938: A girl who drinks the milk on the way tells her mother that the cork flew out of the milk bottle and the milk poured out as she passed a witch's house.
44940: Dogs and magpies announce death during illness. Chasing away a howling dog at the house of a sick person.
44948: A priest gives grains to be placed under the threshold to keep away the mare and people who mean harm; in another case, the advice is to say a prayer.
44965: On a haunted road a man runs into a phantom funeral procession at night and is pushed aside; at that same spot a wheelbarrow also becomes so heavy that it cannot be pushed any further.
45008: A man suddenly sees a light in the meadow. Later the land is bought. When the thickets are cleared, tractors make the same movement the fire made earlier.
45009: A married couple hears knocking and calling but gets no answer, and there is nothing to be seen. Three weeks later the neighbour knocks on the window in the same way to tell them his father has died.
45011: During a fire someone says that two farms will burn down but that a threatened third farm will be spared, because he has seen this before. A prediction by night watchmen who see a glowing red sky that there will be a fire comes true.
45012: Hearing planks being thrown is the voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the building of a house.
45013: A woman sees a small black coffin standing on the threshing floor, while her husband has seen nothing. When their child dies, neighbours bring a small black coffin and put it down on the spot where the mother saw it standing.
45016: Poachers who, after already shooting many hares, see even more hares believe it is witchcraft.
45018: Seeing bridges, a canal and a fire in advance.
45021: Nothing could be done about a bewitched churn. Those who could afford it bought a new churn.
45024: Fear of screeching magpies and howling dogs; they are an omen of a death.
45026: A red dog is seen as the devil; a horse does not dare to pass the red dog; the red dog keeps running alongside the horse and gig.
45027: A man surrounded by cats kicks one of them. A woman regarded as a witch is lame the next day.
45028: Seeing an owl board with a burning post sticking out of it is an omen that the house will burn down.
45031: After money that a deceased woman still owed has been paid, she no longer comes back.
45032: The northern lights are seen as an omen of fire.
45033: Fear of haunting witte wieven (white women).
45035: A warning to cover the rain barrel, or else someone will drown in it, is not heeded. A child drowns in the barrel.
45036: The ghost of a fisherman washed overboard floats through his home town, calls for his mother and stops in front of a house. This means a death by accident in that house.
45037: Whoever crosses a bridge where black cats sometimes jump from railing to railing risks dying.
45039: A road with houses is seen in advance; a woman born with a caul predicts a drowning in the churn.
45041: Fear of a ghost with big ears and a chain on its leg.
45042: A bewitched churn yields no butter.
45044: A man with no fire to light his pipe says that if there were a glowing man, he could do it. The man flees when he meets a glowing man, the devil.
45046: A man sees a house on fire with only a blue flame above the attic. Ten years later the house burns down and someone dies.
45047: A sound as if part of the side wall has fallen, but nothing can be seen. Two weeks later the horse kicks a piece out of the wall.
45048: A howling dog is an omen of a death. An incident in which a dog digs holes through the clay wall of a house and sits howling in the kitchen for many evenings. It stays away once someone has had a fatal fall.
45049: A sound of roof tiles sliding off the roof, but nothing can be seen. Later the carpenter slides roof tiles down and the same sound is heard.
45050: In the French period a man sees a line of dead people coming out of Onstwedde. After the churchyard is later moved, the dead leave Onstwedde at every funeral.
45051: A boy born with a caul sees a hearse with a grey horse in front of it, and tells others. When someone dies, the neighbours want a black horse in front of the wagon. After the black and the brown horse refuse, the grey is put in front of the hearse.
45053: When he snatches an old woman's hat, a man disappears. After coming back he says he was punched and thrown aside.
45054: A man sees a figure at the front door; a maid sees a black figure in the stable, the farmhand sees nothing.
45058: At new moon the ghost of Anna van Ewsum is said to have been seen floating between the manor Nienoord and the church of Midwolde.
45060: Fodder that has spent a night at a witch's bewitches the milk of the cows fed with it, and butter cannot be churned from that milk. After the priest has stirred the churn with a stick, the spell is lifted.
45071: A tenant who could not pay his rent to the lady of the manor is said to have drowned himself. The lady's shade is said to walk about in fog.
45075: A black dog accompanies the narrator and has suddenly vanished.
45088: A woman believes in stories about the full moon; when there is mist she thinks of witte wieven (white women). Then her children are not allowed outside.
45091: A woman dreaming of fish means a death; the size and visibility of the fish determine how far the dead person is from the house or family.
45094: While a woman is baking pancakes from unpaid-for flour, a talking black cat reproaches her for it. The woman hits the cat on the head; the next day the miller's wife, suspected of being a witch, has a swollen face.
45108: The narrator's uncle and aunt heard chains rattling in their house in Westeremden. The family then moved away.
45109: A girl is held captive by the robbers Ellert and Brammert. While they are away, the girl cuts the father's throat. When the two sons discover this, they go after the girl and throw an axe at her, which sticks in the door.
45114: The narrator had an explanatory dream about a fire, which later did happen in her father's grain silo. Also, one day she felt unwell and urged her friends not to take the plane. The plane later crashed.
45125:
The narrator sleeps in a kraal in Senegal and at night sees a little old man standing by her bed, playing drums. The man turned out to be the ghost of the dead medicine man, the healer, of Mombour. Because the narrator was not afraid, the villagers pamper her after she tells them what happened.
A man who proposes marriage to her gives the narrator fertility figurines. Within a few months she is pregnant.
45126: Horseshoe in the milk as protection against bewitchment of the milk and as a means of recognising a witch.
45147: A man sees a flame by some houses, but they are not burning. Later those houses burned down at the same time.
45193: In and around Vlagtwedde stories are told about witte wieven (white women). A play about witte wieven has also been performed. There was a quiet little pub near the border. One evening it gets very busy there. Then a wit wief (white woman) comes in and starts haunting.
45197: While a bird found in a sick person's pillow is being boiled, a woman comes in who takes the pot off the fire and, because of the heat, wipes her face with a handkerchief. The next day her face turns out to be burnt.
45233: When a farmhand is held by the farmer one evening, he rages wildly, and a skin falls into the hearth fire and burns. Then the farmhand calms down and says that he would have had to go about as a werewolf that evening.
45248: By moonlight reeds move even though there is no wind; when approached, a black cat appears and suddenly vanishes.
45251: Omens of misfortune or death; finding a horseshoe brings luck.

45841:
Two wild fellows, Ellert and Brammert, lived as robbers on the heath. They had dug a den themselves. Father and son stretched black threads across the heath with a sheep bell attached, so they could hear passers-by and rob them. On the heath was a valley, the Moordenaarskuil (Murderers' Pit), where they robbed coachmen.
The robbers (giants) wanted a woman to tidy the den, and carried off the runaway Marieke. Marieke escapes by cutting Brammert's throat while shaving him. Ellert then runs after Marieke and throws his axe at the girl, and it sticks in the door. Marieke escapes, and the weeping giant drops dead. The event took place in the Ellertsveld, which got its name from it. The Brammershoopstraat also got its name this way. (Standard Dutch version)

46883:
A farming couple from Westerwolde give a hitchhiker a ride on their cart. The horses pulling the cart become extremely tired, but when the farmer looks to see what could be so heavy, the hitchhiker is nowhere to be seen. Completely exhausted, they reach the farm. The next day they find a dead calf in the stable. The day after, two pigs die, and the day after that several chickens. The couple talk it over and suspect they have the Devil in the house. They call in the help of Hendrik, a devil-banisher.

He has a solution. The threshold of the barn floor is removed and a deep hole is dug there. The best calf is slaughtered and buried under the threshold, and the threshold is put back over it. Then suddenly the hitchhiker is standing there again, and he turns out to be the Devil. He can no longer cross the threshold. Hendrik says he will help him if the Devil first fetches some sand for the farmyard. The two of them go to Wedde, where Hendrik makes the Devil fill a barrel without a bottom. Of course that does not work, and the Devil only manages to make a few small hillocks. Those are the Duvelsbulten.
46884: Hiplichten (will-o'-the-wisps) are the souls of people murdered along the road whose identity could not be traced, and who were therefore buried without a name. 47925:
The Helhond (hellhound) or Kardoes was a ghost dog that accompanied Wodan on his Wild Hunt. With its barking the Helhond announced an imminent death. Farmer Koekenberg once fought the dog, but later nearly died of his wounds.

The statue of the Helhond in De Lutte was commissioned by the textile magnate Molkenboer, who placed it on his property. After his death the statue was placed on the village square.
47926:
The Helhond (hellhound) or Kardoes is known among the people of De Lutte as a ghostly animal. It made a sound like a wolf and was always accompanied by an owl[?]. When people heard the Helhond near the churchyard of De Lutte, they knew someone would soon die.

The farmhand Lambert once fought the Kardoes while out at night and attacked it with his 'lichthak'n', a stick with a hook on it. He managed to flee into the farmhouse and was safe. The next morning he found his stick outside the door, with a jute sack full of boulders tied to it.
48489: The narrator's mother could tell about witte wieven (white women). They were ghosts you could see at dusk.
48649: At the beginning of the 16th century the order of Franciscan nuns was based at Huis Singraven near Denekamp. One evening one of the young nuns could not resist the temptation to go outside the grounds, against the strict rules of the convent. She secretly went to the village and spent the night at the inn, where she enjoyed herself in a worldly way with the men there. When she tried to return to the convent unnoticed, she was betrayed by the creaking stairs. The abbess caught her in this way and decided to set an example to the other nuns. The nun was walled up alive in a niche in the house, where after a while she went mad and starved to death. Her screaming could be heard for days. Since then the ghost of the nun of Singraven has haunted the house, and she sometimes foretells people's deaths.
48650: Mr Roessingh Udink, a former owner of Huis Singraven, died in a strange way. He died of burns after he caught fire while trying, under the influence, to light his cigar on a paraffin lamp. This death is linked to the ghost of the nun of Singraven.
49630: A witch wants to teach her daughter the art so that she too can fly on a broomstick. The formula "out of the chimney, over hedges and bushes" is misspoken by the daughter as "through hedges and bushes". As a result the daughter comes back injured, with torn clothes.
49631: A girl in the schoolyard makes white mice without tails from drops of water from a straw.

As a pledge he must throw a handkerchief to her, and she throws it back with her handprint on it. An alms of wheat must also be doubled.

49637: A haunted barn is consecrated by the priest. After that the haunting stops.

129975: In 1937 a woman had a strange dream of men in skirts standing in rank on the land in front of the house. There was also strange music. Eight years later, in 1945, Scottish Allied soldiers stood in front of the house, exactly as the woman had dreamed in 1937. Eight years earlier she had seen a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event).
130017: The screeching of a tawny owl is seen as a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of death.
130021: The day after a dog has bitten a cat, a woman walks around with a bandage around her head.
130024: The alf (a spirit) looks like a calf, leaps on people, puts its legs on their shoulders, and is heavy. People who carry bread with them are not leapt upon.
130025: No known cases of people who came back after their death. There is, however, a saying showing that dishonest people run the risk of coming back.
130160: A sick man sees a hearse at the neighbour's house and someone being carried inside. The others see nothing. Three days later a hearse carrying the body of the neighbour's dead son stops at the house at the same time, and the body is carried inside.
130162: In the middle of the night someone rings the priest's bell and a voice says he must go to the village of Gammelke. Nobody is to be seen, but the priest sets off, trusting that he will be shown the way. At a house where a light is burning sits a man who tells him the sick person is already dead. The priest goes into the house and is just in time to give the dying person the last rites. The same man says the priest has robbed him of a soul. The priest answers that this was the intention, whereupon the man vanishes. The priest believes that a guardian angel of the deceased warned him.
130163: A man on the road sees fire in a village, but when he gets closer there is nothing to see and nothing has happened. A few weeks later part of the village burns down.
131055:
A man is ferried across the river Vecht by the devil acting as ferryman.

One winter evening a farmer had to go to a hamlet on the other side of the river Vecht. He stayed there chatting with family for too long, and when he finally headed home the weather had not improved. It was raining and a wind had risen. When he reached the river, the ferry turned out to be on the other side, and because of the roar of the storm the farmer could not possibly alert the ferryman, who lived on the other side.
After an hour of shouting in vain, the farmer cried that he wished the devil would come and ferry him across. At once the ferry's chain was loosened with a rattle and the boat began to move. There was no one to be seen, but something or someone skilfully steered the boat through the waves. The farmer was afraid, but did not dare refuse to go aboard.
No one in the area doubted that it had been the devil himself who had ferried the farmer to the other side.
131057: A woman saw a cart without horses that was going very fast. Cars did not exist yet then, but this was probably a voorspooksel or voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the car.
131058:
Voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a fire.

A boy heard noise and saw a great fire at a farm, but suddenly the flames were gone. Later the farm really burned down. The boy had seen a voorspooksel or voorloop.
131059:
On a building site people saw a great many farm carts racing along one after another, a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a train. There were plans for a railway line there, but it was not built at the time.
The narrator seems to want to show with this story how superstitious people used to be.
131060: An old woman was said to be a witch. Towards evening a boatman wanted to take his boat through a swing bridge. The bridge was full of cats. They chased the cats away, but one cat stayed sitting a little longer. This cat finally fled through the chicken hole in the door into the farm where the old woman lived. The boatman was convinced it had been the old woman in the shape of a cat.
131068:
A man born with a caul saw a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a funeral procession.

A man born with a caul could see into the future. One night the man woke up and had to go outside, though he himself did not know why. When he came behind the house he saw a funeral procession approaching across his land. He opened the four gates to let the procession through. 
Two days later a close neighbour died. Because of all the recent rain the road had become impassable, so it was decided to take the hearse from the house of the deceased across the man's land. Would the man be so kind as to open his gates? So exactly one week after his vision the man really did open the four gates and watched the funeral procession pass by.
131069:
An old woman wants to darn stockings on Christmas night, but the lamp keeps going out.

An old woman was darning stockings on Christmas night when the lamp suddenly went out. The woman climbed onto a chair and looked in the lamp: out of paraffin. She refilled the lamp and went on darning, but after one or two stitches the lamp went out again. She climbed onto the chair again: the cotton wick was used up. When she had put a new wick in the lamp and was darning socks again, she clearly heard someone blowing into the lamp. Then she just went to bed.
131133:
Little lights seen at the place where houses would later be built.

A woman said that at her home they used to see little lights burning against the hill. Years later houses were built there (exactly where the lights had burned).
131134:
After her death a woman comes to haunt her husband, who treated her badly.

Grandfather had treated his wife badly. After her death the woman came to haunt her husband. At the same time of day when he had refused to give her water, she came by and asked for water. The neighbours saw only a yellow patch in front of the window, but the man insisted it was his wife's face.
131147: The shepherd of Beerze (a hamlet in the municipality of Ommen) had to move his sheep out of the way of a huge contraption that gave off smoke. A few years later a railway line came at that spot. The man had seen a voorspooksel or voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the train.
131732: A story about how the witte wieven (white women) helped a poor farmer. --- There was a rich, greedy farmer, Völlik, who always took half a metre of his neighbours' land. Every last furrow on his fields actually lay on his neighbours' ground. From the land of one poor neighbour, farmer Jaantie, he even took two furrows' width. At poor farmer Jaantie's something was always wrong: wife ill, children ill, trouble with the animals. In early spring, when the land by the hill had to be worked, farmer Jaantie himself was not well. He had a bad back. His wife Öaltie and the children did what they could, but for the heavy work they depended on help from the neighbours. On top of the hill lived the witte wieven. Normally they did not concern themselves with the people at the foot of the hill, but whether it was because of poor Öaltie's tears or Völlik's injustice, this time they came to help. Farmer Völlik left his plough in the field at night and went home with his horses. The witte wieven lifted the plough and worked farmer Jaantie's land with it. Without making a sound they drew dead-straight furrows and ploughed the ground better than ever. They fetched Jaantie's seed (rye) and sowed it all without spilling a grain. Well before sunrise the plough was back in its place and the witte wieven floated back to the hill. The next morning farmer Völlik could not believe his eyes when he saw farmer Jaantie's land. How had his neighbour managed this in one night? Farmer Völlik set to work on his own land, but after less than twenty metres the plough broke on a big stone. The farmer was furious and stood cursing. The horses grew skittish, and a black horse that was normally very calm began to rear and kicked farmer Völlik in the chest. The man lay there bleeding and groaning. When farmer Völlik was found a few hours later, the horses were standing calmly before the plough. The whole hamlet was shocked when they heard the whole story, farmer Jaantie most of all. All his land had been worked, but there was no trace of footprints or horses' hooves. It took four men to get the big stone out of Völlik's land, and his sons would swear that the stone had not been there before. But everyone understood what had happened and looked at the wisps of mist hanging around the top of the hill.
131923: A man born with a caul saw things before they happened. For example, he foresaw a funeral, a dead person or a fire.
131928: Because of two witches, a man slid with his cart full of manure into a deep ditch. There was a cross on the road.
131933: One evening a man was given a tremendous beating on a sandy road. When they went to look the next day with four or five neighbours, they saw that it was the Lutjekerltje (lutje = little), a little man with horse's legs and human legs. People no longer dared to go along that road in the evening.
131935: If you did not pull the string out of the hole in the door lock at night when you went to bed, no butter would come from the milk; the milk would not thicken.
131953:
A man born with a caul walks one night past a dangerous pool and foresees that an accident will happen there with a horse and cart carrying a bridal couple. The groom will drown in the pool. The man knows this young man and warns him not to marry, because something will happen to him. The young man marries anyway and the prediction of the man born with a caul comes true.
On the wedding day the couple go by horse and cart to the town hall. The horse bolts. The bride manages to jump from the cart in time, but the groom falls into the pool and drowns.
131957: Voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of a funeral procession and a fire.
131968: A man and his neighbour see a light and hear cries for help behind the house. Three years later two boys drown in the canal at that spot. The canal did not even exist yet when the man and his neighbour heard the cries; it still had to be dug.
131969: Abraham foresaw a funeral. He saw people in white caps walking in front of a coffin.
131970:
A woman lies alone in bed because her husband has gone to work very early. Then a black thing comes through the kitchen. The woman hears the dragging of a chain. The thing goes up by the stable and sits on her chest. The woman can no longer say anything.
They lived there for another half year, but nobody wanted to enter the house anymore. The woman never dared to get out of her bed again.
131971:
"Something" with big eyes came up by the roof and walked across it. The people who saw it did not dare run away, because then the creature would come after them.
When the people had fetched a "snidde" (scythe?) to cut off the creature's legs, it was gone.
Some seven or eight people saw it, and none of them dared sleep for the rest of the night. The house later burned down.
131972:
In places where people used to see small lights burning, houses and barracks were later built.
Grandma saw white and red "fireballs" passing by. Later a road was built on which cars with white headlights and red taillights drove past. Grandma also said she saw masts; masts, but no ships. Later telephone poles were put up. Grandma had seen a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event).
131973: A dog that kept barking at the same spot foretold a funeral. The funeral procession passed exactly there. After that the dog was never heard barking again.
131974: Several times people heard doors opening and closing, in the house and in the barn, and they also heard someone walking, but there was no one. Once what they had heard later came true, namely when the doctor had to be fetched one evening.
132018: If a magpie sits on the roof, it is a sign of approaching disaster. But if the magpie sits on the grindstone, nothing will happen.
132019: A halm is a kind of tormenting spirit that hides in a field and jumps on passers-by. If the halm is on you, you had better just keep walking calmly; then it will get off by itself.
132020: You should never walk on a bridle path in the evening, in the dark. You might get a blow that foretells a funeral procession will pass the next day.
132021: One can perhaps defend oneself against witches by boiling a rooster alive.
132039: On Christmas Eve a stranger joins a card game. The stranger turns out to be the devil: one player sees his dog's paw, after which the other players throw down their cards.
132088: On the Zaantiesweggie in Kampen lived a callous farmer who beheaded his beautiful mare in a fit of rage. The mare haunts the place once every hundred years, when the weather and the position of the moon match the circumstances of the horse's death.
132092: The bells of the Sint Odulphus monastery are not consecrated. After a hundred years an old devil gets to take them. He and his nephew play catch with the bells and finally drop them. Where the bells fell, two lakes formed.
132094: A horse pulling a cart of wood stops and refuses to take another step. A big black cat (the devil) turns out to be sitting on top of the load.
132098: A boy goes to sleep in a house that might be haunted and where smugglers come. In the night he is attacked by ghost cats.
132099: A girl cycles home from work. But her bicycle seems to make no progress. She sees a black hand on her arm and is turned around on the road.
206964:
A rhyme to drive away ghosts.

Perhaps:
Old Hunenk has the cold (the cold, fear?, is afraid?).
And I wish the devil came and took old Hunenk away.

It seems the tramp wants to rid the woman of the ghosts by wishing the devil would come and fetch her. And that he then has to get away fast, probably because the woman gets angry.
207164:
The story takes place in Cologne. A dead woman rose from her grave and went back to her house. When she knocked there and said who she was, her husband did not believe her. He said that if it were true, he hoped his horses (greys) would go and look out of the upstairs window. At once the greys climbed up the stairs.
The narrator says there is a house in Cologne where two stone horses' heads look out of the window. His uncle had told him so. But he was not sure whether the house was still standing, because the English had bombed the city during the war.
207243: A man went poaching on a Sunday. He had shot a hare, but when he prodded the animal it ran away. The hare ran past a house where children were playing outside, and they shouted: "Grandmother, run!" The hare was a witch in the shape of a hare.
207261:
There was a ghost haunting a clog maker's house. The clog maker fetched a friar. After two or three days of praying, the friar tied the ghost to a wagon and took it away like that, off the land and to the pool. The ghost was thrown into the pool together with a spint (a measure of volume) of purriezaod (leek seed?).
The ghost could come a little closer each year, but in any case it would not return for years to come (as many years as there were grains of seed??).
207262:
The jack of clubs fetches gin.
A group of soldiers was sitting in a café. One soldier said he could make the jack of clubs fetch gin. The innkeeper knew about such things and said that they would then have to accept the gin. Then a black hand appeared from behind the door with half a litre of gin, but the soldiers just sat laughing. The innkeeper quickly took the gin, otherwise the soldier who had "ordered" it would have died.
207263:
Own funeral seen.
Two brothers, Jan and Drieks, are walking home together. Suddenly Jan hears church bells begin to ring. Then he sees a procession approaching. Drieks hears and sees nothing. Later a new church is built on that spot. Jan is the first to be buried there. Years earlier he had seen his own funeral procession.
207265:
The ghost of a dead man appears to a little boy. The dead man still has a debt to settle, and only an innocent child can do it for him.

Walking past the churchyard one evening, a boy sees a ghost. After that the ghost keeps appearing. His father advises him to ask the ghost what it wants. It turns out the ghost still has a debt to settle. He bought falcons for 250 guilders from a firm in Valkenswaard but never paid for them. An innocent child must help him pay off his debt after all.
The boy's father does not believe it and wants proof. So, at the ghost's request, the boy brings it paper (an old coffee filter) and a (stub of a) pencil, and the ghost writes down his story. If the boy helps the ghost, things will go well for him. If he does not, he will meet with an accident.
Now the father believes it too and arranges the money at the Boerenleenbank. The next day father and son take the train to Valkenswaard. The name of the firm is still known, but the name of the burgomaster cannot be found anywhere in the books.
In the end father and son donate the money for the debt to a good cause through the church and return home.
The boy sees the ghost once more after that. The ghost thanks him and his father and flies away as a white bird. The boy's little sister saw it too.
207294:
A maid saw things before they happened. She foresaw the death of a farmhand. The lady of the house did not believe her, because the farmhand was as fit as a fiddle. But the farmhand fell from the hay wagon and died.
The maid had also seen that the master's white horse would pull the hearse. The lady of the house asked her husband to harness the brown horse, to show the maid that not everything she saw happened exactly so. But the brown horse was so restless in front of the hearse that in the end they had to use the white horse after all. So everything the maid had seen came true exactly.
207303:
The maid Janna was clairvoyant. She often saw things before they happened. One day she was very sad because she had seen that the master would die. Nobody believed it, but one morning the master was indeed found dead in bed. He had been given an ointment by a quack for a wound on his leg. Because of it the wound had closed too quickly and the "bad substances" in the leg could no longer get out.
Now that Janna had been proven right again, the other maid no longer wanted to work with her. Janna was allowed to stay and the other maid found a position elsewhere.
209511: Jan van Deest was coming back late from the mill. On the Kerkdijk, in pitch darkness, the wheel of his wheelbarrow slips into a hole up to the hub three times. Each time he lifts it, a black cat runs under his feet. He gives the animal a tremendous kick, whereupon the witch (for the black cat was a witch) says: "Do that again, Dees, and it will go badly for you," and Jan quickly ran off. He had never run so fast and never again went home from the mill so late.
209576:
Bart, a boy from Beek, is going home late in the evening from Zeddam. His friends ask whether he is afraid of the boelekerel (bogeyman), since he is in such a hurry, but Bart says it is because of the White Lady of the Berg. He wants to invite her to dance with him at the Whitsun feast.
When he reaches the Berg, he sees a white figure: the lady. She beckons him to stop. She seizes Bart and drags him into a whirling round dance. In the end Bart is left as limp as a dishcloth. His horse has gone home, and his household come looking for him and bring him home. But Bart never recovers and dies within three days.
209577:
Faust was Catholic, but became godless by reading books.
Faust sells his soul to the devil and may live for twenty-five years as if he were twenty-five years old. He lives it up with women and drink, horses and money, and plays all kinds of tricks. When the twenty-five years are over, Faust gives a big party for his family. At the party the devil comes to fetch him.
The family wants to bury Faust in a Catholic churchyard, but a storm rises. The priest flies over the hedge, the coffin flies through the air and the grave fills up with sand again.
209611:
By means of a little doll a witch can do two things at once, in two different places.
---
A woman who could do magic asked a tailor to make a suit for her husband. Meanwhile she went to churn the milk and work in the vegetable garden. When the tailor looked outside he saw the woman in the garden, while the milk was also being churned. A little doll turned out to be working the milk. The tailor put the doll in his pocket and went on with his work.
When the woman saw that the churning had stopped she began calling “Pierefietje”. The louder the woman called, the harder the doll danced in the tailor's trouser pocket; the butter ran out of his trousers. The tailor quickly threw the doll away, grabbed his things and ran home.
209685:
An altar boy had heard that witches could not leave the church if a dime that had first lain under a missal was placed under the threshold. He tried it and the story proved true. After Mass some people stayed seated in the church and could only leave once the dime was removed.
But to protect himself from the witches' revenge, the altar boy had to carry the dime with him from then on. He did so. But when he got married he forgot to put the dime in his wedding suit. On the way to his bride he was seized by witches and dragged through hedges and bushes until not a scrap of flesh or bone was left on him.
210366: You should not walk in the middle of the road at night, because you could collide with a hearse. That happened to Berend when he was on his way home drunk. He injured his leg and suffered from it for the rest of his life. No one could heal his leg.
210367:
Some people could tell in advance where an accident would happen or where a house would burn down. This was not dangerous.
There were also [women?] who flew through the air and gathered at their own spot in the field. They were not very dangerous either.
210368:
The older people talked a lot about witches, ghosts, weerlopen (werewolves) and the devil. Then a friar had to come from Germany who was very good at driving such beings into the Zwarte Meer. In the water they could do no harm. But no people were allowed to be present.
In beds and pillows, especially children's, heksenkransen (witches' wreaths) were sometimes found. Then people looked carefully to see whether there was an old aunt who had burns on her face or hands.
210375:
Some land surveyors in the peat country were dishonest and took bribes. They took land from one person and gave it to another. Such people did not go to heaven, but were sent back to earth to measure the land again, and better. However, they could never find the beginning or the end of the field, so they were doomed to wander forever.
On a misty day, pious doctor Harm met such a damned land surveyor in the field: a black fellow with horse's legs, horns and a rattling chain. The monster could make itself small and then large again and pulled horrible grimaces and faces, but Harm would not be frightened. But when the surveyor tried to kick him in the stomach, he took the Seventh Book of Moses from his pocket and read a passage from it to exorcise the evil one. Harm ordered the devil to go back where he came from, and the devil vanished in a cloud of sulphur.
210376: If the churning would not come and there was no butter, the churn was bewitched. A red-hot poker was then put into it, and afterwards people looked to see whether the person suspected of bewitching the churn had black marks on the face or hands.
210381: Not familiar with moving boundary stones.
210402: Dokter Harm was not really a proper doctor, but he did do doctor-like work now and then. He was good at pulling teeth and was called when a cow, goat or other animal was sick. He would then make crosses on the animal. Animals, like people, could be possessed by the devil. Once a goat was held under water for so long to drown the evil spirit inside it that the goat itself died as well.
210410: People sometimes saw strange things, such as little lights, at places where something would later be built, such as a canal, a road, houses or a whole town. A fire was sometimes seen in advance too. Often such a house or farm did indeed burn down later.
210859: People used to experience all sorts of things. Sometimes they frightened themselves and others. They heard knocking, saw people carrying a coffin, saw something in the form of a black dog or a black fellow. People often saw a big fellow walking around with a dog. Later a minister came who did indeed walk through the village with his dog.
210863: Near Montferland people sometimes heard the juffer (maiden) laughing and singing. Some have also seen her. But you must not come too close, for then she would pull you into the water.
